Peacock Orders the First Fast & Furious Series, With Vin Diesel Producing
Universal Television's series from co-showrunners Mike Daniels and Wolfe Coleman premieres in 2028, the year Fast Forever ends the film franchise on March 17, and three more series projects are in development.
Peacock greenlit its first Fast & Furious series, Deadline reports, extending a franchise that has grossed more than $7 billion worldwide over 25 years. Vin Diesel, who announced the project at NBCUniversal's May upfront, executive produces alongside Neal H. Moritz, Chris Morgan and others. Diesel said he agreed to a TV move only after Universal film chief Donna Langley also took oversight of NBCUniversal's TV operation, because the characters would be "protected in the TV space." Three more series are in development, from Nick Wooton and Charmaine DeGraté, Ingrid Escajeda, and Joe Henderson.
Potential Talent Implication: Vin Diesel signed off on Fast & Furious television only after the executive who runs the films also took over TV, and an executive producer credit on every extension may be where a franchise star's approval gets paid.
The Facts
  • Series order: Peacock, first Fast & Furious TV series; studio Universal Television; premiere set for 2028.
  • Writers and co-showrunners: Mike Daniels (PONIES, Shades of Blue, Sons of Anarchy, NBC's upcoming The Rockford Files) and Wolfe Coleman (9-1-1: Lone Star, Shades of Blue).
  • Executive producers: Daniels, Coleman, Vin Diesel and One Race's Sam Vincent, Original Film's Neal H. Moritz and Pavun Shetty, Jeff Kirschenbaum, Chris Morgan.
  • Diesel at the May upfront: "As you all know, we are very precious about these movies but over the last decade, we've realized that the fans have wanted more." He said the integrity of the characters "will be protected in the TV space" once Donna Langley also took oversight of NBCUniversal TV last year.
  • Three other Fast & Furious series in the works: Nick Wooton (The Endgame) with Charmaine DeGraté (House of the Dragon); Ingrid Escajeda (Griselda); Joe Henderson (Lucifer).
  • Film franchise: more than $7 billion global box office over 25 years; Fast Forever, the 11th and final film, set for March 17, 2028.

FX Has Not Renewed Ryan Murphy's The Shards, and Nobody Outside Disney Has the Numbers
The Shards averaged 237,000 viewers in first FX airings, never made Nielsen's streaming top 10, and has no renewal three weeks after a cliffhanger finale; Murphy's The Beauty released its cast in July.
FX has made no decision on The Shards, Ryan Murphy's ongoing adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' novel, more than three weeks after its finale, and has released no streaming data, The Hollywood Reporter reports. It is the second Murphy-produced FX series this year to end on a cliffhanger without a pickup: The Beauty ended in March and released its cast in July. Murphy has a large overall deal with Disney's 20th Television, and THR writes that a renewal may reflect those relationships more than a hit.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney holds the only streaming numbers on The Shards, and without them Ryan Murphy's case for a second season rests on his 20th Television overall deal and his history at FX.
The Facts
  • Status: no renewal decision from FX more than three weeks after the season finale, which ended on a cliffhanger.
  • Ratings: average 237,000 viewers for initial FX airings; never appeared in Nielsen's streaming top 10; FX has released no data of its own.
  • FX precedent: Adults and The Lowdown were renewed months after their first seasons ended.
  • Murphy's FX record this year: The Beauty ended in early March and its cast was released in July; Love Story, which FX cited as a ratings success, also has not been renewed.
  • Anthology gaps: more than two years between American Horror Story seasons (new season premiered Sept. 24); nearly seven years between Feud seasons one and two.
  • Murphy has a big overall deal with Disney's 20th Television; THR notes his 20th-produced shows kept getting new seasons even while he was based at Netflix.

Sony Plans a Spider-Man: Brand New Day Re-Release With Footage Cut From the First Run
Brand New Day stands at $950.7 million domestic and $2.5 billion worldwide; Avengers: Endgame Encore opened to $26 million the prior weekend with new footage teasing Avengers: Doomsday.
Sony is planning to reissue Spider-Man: Brand New Day in theaters with new footage, TheWrap reports, following Deadline's first report; Sony did not comment. The film opened to a summer-record $360 million and is the all-time domestic leader, ahead of Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Deadline speculated the footage could include a cut hospital scene with Rosario Dawson as Claire Temple, replaced in the release by Jon Bernthal's Punisher. Director Destin Daniel Cretton has said a tested version ran 30 minutes longer. TheWrap notes a reissue could carry the film past $1 billion domestic, which no film has done.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney and Sony are now selling cut footage back to theaters, and for talent with box office backend on Brand New Day, a reissue's gross and any newly used scenes may run through terms written for the original release.
The Facts
  • Plan: Sony reissue of Spider-Man: Brand New Day in theaters with new footage; details not yet known; Sony had no comment (TheWrap, "has learned"; Deadline reported first).
  • Box office to date: $360 million opening (summer record); $950.7 million domestic; $2.5 billion worldwide; all-time domestic champion, passing Star Wars: The Force Awakens last month.
  • Possible footage (Deadline speculation): a hospital scene of Rosario Dawson as Claire Temple caring for Tom Holland's Peter Parker, cut and replaced with Jon Bernthal's Punisher.
  • Cretton previously told TheWrap a tested version ran 30 minutes longer; he called the theatrical cut his preferred version.
  • Precedent: Disney and Marvel Studios re-released Avengers: Endgame as Avengers: Endgame Encore to $26 million, with new footage teasing December's Avengers: Doomsday.

Shortical Says AI-Made Shows Doubled Its Microdrama Business, Now Headed to $100 Million
Mansa, co-founded by David Oyelowo and Nate Parker, makes vertical series for $100,000 to $250,000 each; Shortical's Guy Shimoni says studios now call him and has a James Franco series in the works.
At TheWrap's TheGrill 2026, Shortical founder and CEO Guy Shimoni said the company is set to reach $100 million in revenue by year-end and that the business doubled after it began releasing AI-made content, which let it add genres such as superheroes and longer serialized shows. Shortical releases a feature-length AI film, Inevitable, this month. Shimoni said Hollywood players that dismissed microdramas 18 months ago now come to him because of the revenue. aTwist CEO Jana Winograde, a former TV executive, said her platform casts mostly vertical-native stars and unknowns, with some celebrity projects.
Potential Talent Implication: Shortical credits AI-made shows for doubling a business on track for $100 million, and actors and writers taking microdrama work for the break are selling to a platform that already has a cheaper option on its own slate.
The Facts
  • Shortical (Guy Shimoni, founder and CEO): set to do $100 million in revenue by end of 2026; "Our business has doubled ever since we started rolling out AI content"; feature-length AI film Inevitable releasing later in October; microdrama series in the works with James Franco; now producing longer series, not only 60-minute total runs.
  • Shimoni: "18 months ago when we started talking about short form content, mobile streaming, microdramas, no one wanted to hear about it... Now everyone is knocking on our door."
  • Mansa (David Oyelowo, Nate Parker co-founders; Parker is CEO): vertical productions budgeted at $100,000 to $250,000; platform built for Black creative voices.
  • Parker: "Not everyone can make a film for $5 million, $10 million, $20 million."
  • aTwist (Jana Winograde, CEO and co-founder, former TV executive): launched early September with traditional entertainment partnerships; a family series with Mario Lopez and a musical microseries from Jesse Tyler Ferguson; mostly vertical stars and unknown talent on screen.
  • Oyelowo: microdramas offer "a fiscally responsible, possible and plausible way to put people to work to cultivate talent" amid industry contraction.

A Judge Threw Out Penske's Antitrust Case Over Google's AI Summaries of Its Articles
Judge Amit Mehta ruled that a publisher's expectation of search traffic is not an agreement; Penske, which owns Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter, can refile because the dismissal was without prejudice.
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media's suit against Google over AI Overviews, ruling Wednesday that antitrust law does not apply, TheWrap reports. Penske argued Google unlawfully conditions inclusion in search results on letting its articles feed AI summaries, said it lost revenue, and asked that Google be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or train AI on them. Mehta wrote that "an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works." Mehta dismissed without prejudice, so Penske may refile.
Potential Talent Implication: A federal judge would not let Penske use antitrust law to make Google pay for AI summaries of its articles, and for creators whose work feeds AI tools, payment may now depend on a license negotiated up front.
The Facts
  • Ruling: U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media Corporation's lawsuit against Google on Wednesday (Sept. 30); antitrust laws do not apply to AI Overviews of news articles.
  • Mehta: "Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an 'expectation' that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free. But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works."
  • Penske's claims (filed 2025): Google leverages search by including only publishers that permit AI-summary use; about a fifth of Google searches linking to sites show Overviews; Google should be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or use them to train AI; PMC alleged lost revenue.
  • Co-plaintiff: Chegg, alleging Google illegally scraped its content.
  • Penske owns The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Variety, Rolling Stone, Gold Derby, Billboard, IndieWire and Artforum.
  • Dismissal was not with prejudice; Penske may refile. PMC, Google and Chegg did not immediately comment.

Paramount and Warner Bros. Are Now One Company: Skydance
David Ellison named the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery "Skydance" on X Friday, ahead of the $110 billion merger's expected Oct. 6 close after a year of pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay.
David Ellison announced Friday that the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will be called Skydance once their $110 billion merger closes Oct. 6, following a year-long pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay from 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America. Ellison said the name avoids favoring either century-old studio: "We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one." Paramount separately priced $41.4 billion in senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion term loan B to finance the deal. Discovery Communications, public since 2008, will no longer carry its name forward.
Potential Talent Implication: Skydance opens for business carrying tens of billions in new debt, which means a highly leveraged buyer negotiating every future deal from a cost-discipline posture.
The Facts
  • Merger value: $110 billion; expected close date Oct. 6, 2026.
  • Delay: one-year pursuit by Ellison, plus a two-month hold from antitrust suits by 12 state attorneys general and the WGA, resolved via a 5-year consent decree requiring separation of Paramount/WBD operations in several business areas.
  • Financing: Paramount Skydance Corporation priced $41.4 billion and €885 million in senior secured notes offerings and an $8.5 billion and €850 million term loan B facility (announced via SEC filing Sept. 30, 2026).
  • Naming history: Skydance's August 2025 acquisition of Paramount was initially styled "Paramount, a Skydance Corporation," later "Paramount Skydance Corporation." Colloquial names "WarnaMount" and "ParaBros" had circulated in the absence of an official name.
  • Discovery Communications went public in 2008; the Discovery brand will not appear in the new corporate name.
  • Quote, Ellison: "What once was the peak, is now just the beginning... Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling."
· Deadline (Dade Hayes); corroborated Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, The Verge · 2026-10-02 · https://deadline.com/2026/10/paramount-warner-bros-skydance-david-ellison-1237143716/ · Provenance: named-exec-quote source ↗
Warner Bros. Film Chiefs De Luca and Abdy Are Out
Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy learned from news reports, not a call from David Ellison, that they will not run film at the merged company, with Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg taking over the combined unit instead.
Warner Bros. film chairs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy will not join the merged company, Deadline and Puck reported, with Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg set to run the combined unit's roughly 30 releases a year instead. De Luca and Abdy, under contract through 2030, could get a producing deal rather than report to the new chairs. Their Warner Bros. slate carries 56% of the combined company's 71 dated features through 2028, plus Oscar winners One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons, following a 2025 high and a 2026 marked by underperformers Digger, The Bride and Supergirl.
Potential Talent Implication: Any filmmaker whose deal was built on De Luca and Abdy's taste now negotiates with Greenstein and Goldberg instead, and the 71-picture dated slate they built is the one piece of leverage that survives the exit intact.
The Facts
  • De Luca and Abdy have run Warner Bros.' film division since June 2022, after jumping from MGM following Amazon's acquisition of that studio; they re-upped their WBD contracts through 2030 under David Zaslav.
  • Per Deadline: neither executive received a call from Ellison about their status; they learned from news reports the night before this story published.
  • Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, current Paramount Motion Picture co-chairs, are poised to run the combined Paramount Warner Bros. film unit, per multiple sources.
  • The combined company inherits ~71 dated features through 2028, with 56% generated by De Luca/Abdy's Warner Bros., plus the $4.37 billion globally grossing 2025 slate they built.
  • Oscar-winning titles in that slate: One Battle After Another, Sinners (rights revert to director Ryan Coogler) and Weapons.
  • De Luca/Abdy's contracts call for them to report to the CEO, not other motion-picture chairs; reporting into Greenstein/Goldberg is described as an unlikely scenario. A producing contract at the new company is a possible alternative.
  • 2026 box office under De Luca/Abdy: no release above $100 million domestic, including underperformers The Bride and Supergirl, plus the as-yet-unreleased Digger (tracking toward a possible $30 million worldwide opening or less).
  • Under De Luca/Abdy, Warner Bros. earned 30 Oscar nominations this year (tying its 2005 record) and won 11, including Best Picture for One Battle After Another.
  • Per Puck: the executive chart for the new company is expected within days; Paramount declined to comment on De Luca/Abdy's status.
· Deadline (exclusive); corroborated Puck (Matthew Belloni), Variety, The Hollywood Reporter · 2026-10-02 · https://deadline.com/2026/10/michael-de-luca-pamela-abdy-exit-warner-bros-paramount-merger-1237145206/ · Provenance: trade-rumor source ↗
Barbie 2 Is Stuck Because CAA Wants a Bigger Check
CAA's Bryan Lourd sought fees for Greta Gerwig, Noah Baumbach, Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling so high that a Barbie sequel's breakeven topped $700 million, and Warner Bros. let the talks collapse rather than pay.
A Barbie sequel has been dead at Warner Bros. since CAA's Bryan Lourd, representing director Greta Gerwig and co-writer Noah Baumbach, sought fees for them, star Margot Robbie, co-star Ryan Gosling and Mattel so high that the film's breakeven point topped $700 million, Puck reported. Talks broke down, Barbie toy sales have fallen back to pre-movie levels, and Mattel's stock has languished enough that a shareholder called for a company sale in May. Lourd appears to be waiting for David Ellison and incoming co-CEO Ynon Kreiz to restart talks once the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger closes.
Potential Talent Implication: Lourd is betting that a merged, better-funded Skydance will pay the price he already named rather than relitigate the fee, and a representative's leverage over a stalled deal only grows once the buyer across the table changes.
The Facts
  • Lourd (CAA) poached Gerwig and Baumbach from UTA for the sequel and then demanded fees for the pair, plus Robbie, Gosling and Mattel, that pushed the film's breakeven point past $700 million at the box office.
  • Negotiations broke down; the sequel is "dead for now" at Warner Bros., per Puck.
  • Barbie toy sales have fallen back to pre-movie-release levels; Mattel's overall share price has been "languishing."
  • A major Mattel shareholder called for a sale of the company in May 2026, according to The Wall Street Journal (as cited by Puck).
  • Incoming Paramount-WBD co-CEO Ynon Kreiz previously ran Mattel (2018-2026) and has prior history with Lourd's client relationships via that role; Puck's read is that Lourd is "biding his time" until Ellison, and now Kreiz, are positioned to write the checks.
  • The nugget surfaced inside Puck's broader report on Warner Bros. film leadership changes following the Paramount merger close.

Casey Bloys Will Decide What Gets Made Across HBO Max and Paramount+
Casey Bloys is the presumed head of the combined streaming operation after Paramount's Cindy Holland departed this week, putting one executive in charge of greenlights across HBO, HBO Max and Paramount+.
Casey Bloys, HBO and HBO Max content chief, is the presumed head of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. streaming operation after Paramount's direct-to-consumer chair Cindy Holland exited this week, Deadline reported. Bloys would not confirm his title but said HBO Max and Paramount+ may be bundled rather than merged. His core team, including drama chief Francesca Orsi and comedy chief Amy Gravitt, is expected to move with him; Orsi turned down a top job at Amazon MGM Studios this summer partly over WBD's strict contract terms. Netflix's Ted Sarandos and Disney's Dana Walden both praised Bloys publicly this week.
Potential Talent Implication: Every creator with a show at HBO, Max or Paramount+ now has one person deciding whether it gets made, which makes Bloys's own taste the thing to understand before pitching there.
The Facts
  • Bloys has survived two prior mergers: AT&T's acquisition of Time Warner, and Discovery's acquisition of WarnerMedia in 2022.
  • Cindy Holland, Paramount's Chair of Direct-to-Consumer, exited earlier this week, which Deadline frames as the deciding factor leaving Bloys as presumed head of the combined streaming operation; the merger formally closes Oct. 6.
  • Bloys hinted at Bloomberg Screentime that HBO Max and Paramount+ "may be bundled" rather than merged into one service.
  • Expected to move with Bloys: head of drama Francesca Orsi, head of comedy Amy Gravitt, and HBO Max's Sarah Aubrey (The Pitt, Hacks, the upcoming Harry Potter series, and international). Orsi was approached for a top programming job at Amazon MGM Studios this summer but stayed, partly because of WBD's strict contract terms.
  • At Bloomberg Screentime, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos called Bloys "a super talented guy" who "is going to be in a very good position wherever he goes," without directly addressing reported Netflix-Bloys talks. Disney's Dana Walden called him "an incredibly savvy executive."
  • Bloys's current contract runs through 2027 and is said to include a stipulation that he reports directly to the CEO, a condition Ellison kept in order to retain him and his team.
  • Paramount-WBD's incoming leadership: Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz are both set to have businesses reporting jointly to them.
  • Bloys on broadening HBO's slate to include CBS procedurals/sitcoms and Paramount+ mass-appeal titles (Taylor Sheridan/101 Studios' Landman and MobLand; Tyler Perry's Sistas; UFC): "There are no plans to dilute the HBO brand," he said in 2018 of the AT&T deal, a position he now describes as having evolved through a decade of "broadening out."
  • Overlap already exists: several Cindy Holland-era Paramount+ greenlights, including Discretion (Nicole Kidman, Elle Fanning), are described as "HBO-like" shows that could fit either brand.

Disney Licenses Percy Jackson and Ice Age to Netflix to Sell Its Next Releases
Percy Jackson Seasons 1-2 and all five Ice Age films stream on Netflix globally from Oct. 4 in three-month windows timed to Season 3 on Disney+ and Ice Age: Boiling Point in theaters.
Disney Entertainment signed an expansive licensing deal with Netflix, Variety reports. Two Disney+ properties get three-month promotional windows on Netflix ahead of new installments: Percy Jackson and the Olympians before its Nov. 20 Season 3, and the five Ice Age films before Ice Age: Boiling Point opens Feb. 5, 2027. Current 20th Television series Will Trent and Shifting Gears go to Netflix globally, Tracker internationally on a multiyear term, and Pixar and Walt Disney Animation films including Soul and Elio follow in early 2027. Every title stays on Disney+ and Hulu.
Potential Talent Implication: Percy Jackson's first two seasons are now a three-month ad on Netflix for Season 3, and for anyone with backend on a Disney title the question is how that license fee shows up in the participation statement.
The Facts
  • Deal: Disney Entertainment and Netflix, expansive content licensing agreement covering library titles and current-season TV, for varying periods (Variety exclusive).
  • Promotional windows (three months each, from Oct. 4, global): Percy Jackson and the Olympians S1-2 ahead of S3 on Disney+ Nov. 20; Ice Age (2002), The Meltdown (2006), Dawn of the Dinosaurs (2009), Continental Drift (2012), Collision Course (2016) ahead of Ice Age: Boiling Point in theaters Feb. 5, 2027.
  • 20th Television current series: Will Trent S1-4 (global, Nov. 3, ahead of S5 on ABC early 2027); Shifting Gears S1-2 (U.S. Dec. 1, international January, ahead of S3 on ABC early 2027); Tracker S1-3 (international outside U.S., Feb. 26, 2027, multiyear term; S4 premieres on CBS Oct. 4).
  • Disney-branded non-franchise animation from early 2027, global: Soul, Elio, Raya and the Last Dragon and others.
  • Library series: Felicity (U.S. Oct. 7), Revenge (global), Army Wives (global), Fresh Off the Boat (U.S. and select regions), This Is Us (international).
  • Joins prior Disney licenses on Netflix: Grey's Anatomy, Arrested Development, Scandal, Black-ish.
  • Variety: Disney generates "millions in incremental revenue"; all titles stay on Disney+ and Hulu; Netflix has 325 million-plus subscribers.

Paramount's New Co-CEO Gets a $31.5 Million Signing Bonus
Ynon Kreiz will collect a $31.5 million signing bonus and at least $35.1 million a year in total pay by 2027 under the five-year contract Paramount disclosed for its incoming co-CEO.
Paramount disclosed in an SEC filing that incoming co-CEO Ynon Kreiz will get a $31.5 million signing bonus in restricted stock, a base salary rising from $3.5 million to $5 million once the Warner Bros. Discovery merger closes, and an annual bonus rising to $4.9 million. He is also eligible for 2.6 million shares of Class B stock and annual equity grants worth $20.1 million starting in year two. The former Mattel CEO's new pay lands at or above the high end of his Mattel compensation, which ranged from $15.1 million to $37.8 million a year.
Potential Talent Implication: Kreiz's package shows what a merged, debt-heavy company will still pay for certainty at the top, which sets the real ceiling for any executive or talent retention deal negotiated at the new Skydance this year.
The Facts
  • Signing bonus: $31.5 million, paid in restricted stock units (RSUs).
  • Employment contract start date: Monday, Oct. 5, 2026; elevated post-merger terms take effect once the $110 billion deal closes (expected Oct. 6).
  • Base salary: $3.5 million pre-merger, rising to $5 million after close.
  • Annual bonus target: $1.5 million pre-merger, rising to $4.9 million after close.
  • Equity: eligible for 2.6 million shares of Class B stock plus a separate 1.25 million-share award; within 15 days of merger close, an RSU grant worth up to $5.1 million (prorated); starting Oct. 5, 2027 (contract's first anniversary), annual equity awards worth $20.1 million.
  • Paramount's board approved Kreiz's appointment Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026; his exit from Mattel was announced the morning of Sept. 30 (Wednesday), with his new Paramount post revealed later that day.
  • Prior Mattel compensation: $18.9 million (2023), $37.8 million (2024), $15.1 million (2025).
  • Kreiz, 61, previously led Endemol Group, Maker Studios and Fox Kids Europe; the filing cites "extensive leadership experience in the media and entertainment industry" as grounds for also naming him to the combined company's board.
  • The merger was held up roughly two months by a legal challenge from 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America before clearing its last hurdle.

Netflix's Stranger Things Creators Left Because It Doesn't Make Movies
Ted Sarandos said the Duffer Brothers left their decade-long Netflix deal for a four-year Paramount deal, and Shawn Levy left for Disney's 20th Television, because both wanted to make theatrical movies Netflix does not.
Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos told The Hollywood Reporter that Stranger Things creators Matt and Ross Duffer left their decade-long Netflix deal for a four-year film and TV deal at Paramount because they want theatrical movies, not more television. Shawn Levy, who directed for Netflix a decade and is now making Star Wars: Starfighter for Lucasfilm, left for Disney's 20th Television for the same reason. The sale follows Imagine's thin run of hits since the 2000s (its last global theatrical success was 2016's "Inferno") and a strained relationship between Raine and Grazer, who is negotiating the deal himself. A prior planned sale to Centricus Asset Management at a $700 million valuation fell apart in 2024 as investor interest in production companies cooled.
Potential Talent Implication: A new, private-equity-backed owner at Imagine resets who controls the company's overhead, its library monetization and its next production deal, at a moment when comparable shingles (SpringHill, Hartbeat, Hello Sunshine) have all been forced into mergers, downsizing, or unit closures.
The Facts
  • Raine, led by co-founder Joe Ravitch and partner Erik Hodge, is exiting its 51% ownership of Imagine Entertainment, purchased for $100 million in 2016; the buyer is a private-equity-backed marketing firm whose name and the price could not be learned.
  • An Imagine representative called TheWrap's report "factually inaccurate" while declining to give further detail.
  • Imagine has been exploring a sale since at least 2024; a planned $700 million sale to Centricus Asset Management fell apart that year as interest in production companies cooled.
  • China Media Capital invested $100 million alongside Raine in 2016; FountainVest Partners invested another $100 million in 2018. By 2021 Imagine was valued around $850 million.
  • Imagine's last global theatrical hit was 2016's "Inferno"; 2025's "After the Hunt" (Julia Roberts, Andrew Garfield) grossed just $9 million worldwide, and Howard's "Eden" (Sydney Sweeney) made $2.8 million after Vertical picked it up. The last Imagine film to cross $100 million domestically was 2017's "American Made" ($135 million on a $50 million budget).
  • Comparable independent production companies have struggled: LeBron James' SpringHill Company (once valued at $750 million) merged into Fulwell 73 in 2024; Kevin Hart's Hartbeat (once valued at $650 million) has downsized repeatedly; Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine shuttered its kids and family unit in 2023.
  • Howard, 72, is in post-production on the Amazon MGM Afghanistan war drama "Alone at Dawn" (Adam Driver); Grazer, 75, continues producing, including Netflix docs "Marty, Life Is Short" and "Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing." Upcoming Imagine titles: 20th Century's "Whalefall" (October theatrical), Amazon MGM's "How to Rob a Bank" (David Leitch), Netflix's "The Mosquito Bowl" (Pete Berg), and the Apple series "Wild Things" (Andrew Garfield, Jude Law). A Howard-Jim Carrey "Grinch" sequel is in early development.
  • Raine has separately been active in sports and gambling deals, including DraftKings, and most recently a $750 million catalog acquisition fund with Ares for music/artist-management company Firebird.

Donna Langley Says Universal Is Deliberately Undoing Its Own Short-Window Training

The Facts
  • Universal struck a deal with AMC Theatres at the onset of COVID-19 allowing PVOD release as early as 17 days after theatrical, which triggered industry-wide windowing experimentation; Universal announced a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window earlier in 2026, ending that era.

  • Hodge: "There's a lot of opportunity around the migration of traditional talent, traditional content, onto YouTube." Apple Studios Visual Effects Workers Win Their First IATSE Contract
Apple Studios visual effects workers ratified their first IATSE contract, securing minimum rates, AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, employer-paid health and retirement benefits, and overtime and rest protections matching editorial crews.
IATSE announced Apple Studios VFX workers secured their first union contract, following the same path as VFX workers on "Avatar" and at Marvel and Disney, who ratified their first contracts last year. The agreement sets minimum rates per covered title tied to annual increases matching the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, overtime including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays, employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care and pension benefits plus a defined-contribution retirement plan (effective retroactively to all hours worked since January 1), AI protections from the Basic Agreement, turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties, and hazard pay for dangerous on-set conditions. IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb said VFX workers have long powered major productions "without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues."
Potential Talent Implication: A second major platform's VFX workforce organizing in successive years, each contract carrying explicit AI guardrails from the Basic Agreement, establishes AI-use protections as a now-standard term below-the-line crews expect on any production regardless of which studio or platform is financing it.
The Facts
  • Apple Studios visual effects workers secured their first IATSE contract, per IATSE's September 30 announcement.
  • Contract establishes minimum rates for every covered title; annual minimum-rate increases match those negotiated in the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement.
  • Workers secured minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, and overtime protections including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays.
  • Employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care, pension benefits, and a defined-contribution retirement savings plan; employer contributions to health/retirement plans apply retroactively to all hours worked since January 1, 2026.
  • Contract incorporates AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, plus daily/weekly turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties for violated lunch breaks, and additional pay for hazardous on-set conditions.
  • IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb: "For too long, visual effects workers have powered some the industry's biggest productions without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues. It is long past time to fix that."
  • Last year, VFX workers on "Avatar" and those working at Marvel and Disney ratified their first labor contracts, including overtime pay, Motion Picture Industry Pension and Health Plan eligibility, meal penalties, rest periods and turnaround times; the Disney/Marvel contract included 4% and 3.5% raises in its first two years, matching IATSE-negotiated raises.

Endeavor's Audacious Carl Icahn Defense
Endeavor and Silver Lake sued Carl Icahn and dozens of investment funds on September 21, asking Delaware's Chancery Court to strip appraisal rights from investors who bought in after the 2024 take-private deal solely to sue for more money.
Endeavor's 2025 take-private squeeze-out produced what the company calls the largest appraisal proceeding in Delaware history: roughly 80% of its public float was submitted for appraisal after shares jumped on TKO's value post-announcement. Icahn, Troluce Capital and Pentwater Capital bought in afterward on the theory litigation could extract another $2-3 billion above the $27.50-a-share deal price. Endeavor's filing alleges Troluce raised nearly $1 billion for a dedicated appraisal fund and that a January 2025 meeting was literally titled "Appraisal for Dummies." Icahn's lawyers call the new suit "procedurally bizarre."
Potential Talent Implication: Endeavor wants Delaware to void appraisal claims built on shares bought specifically to sue: a ruling either way resets how much money coordinated investors can extract from a future agency take-private, changing the math the next time WME, CAA or a rival goes private.
The Facts
  • Endeavor and Silver Lake filed suit against Carl Icahn and dozens of investment funds in Delaware Chancery Court on September 21, seeking to bar investors who bought Endeavor shares after the take-private deal was announced from pursuing appraisal rights.
  • The 2024 go-private deal valued Endeavor at $27.50 a share, paid when the deal closed in early 2025; shares then rose on the strength of Endeavor's majority stake in TKO (parent of WWE and UFC), drawing in appraisal-seeking investors.
  • Approximately 80% of Endeavor's public float was submitted for appraisal, per Endeavor's filing.
  • Troluce Capital Advisors (co-founded by Jonathan Christodoro, a former Icahn lieutenant) allegedly raised nearly $1 billion for a special-purpose appraisal fund and recruited other firms and an unnamed global financial institution.
  • Filings describe investor roundtables including a January 23, 2025 meeting called "Appraisal for Dummies," attended by representatives of Icahn, Troluce and their lawyers.
  • Icahn allegedly amassed his position mostly in the final 10 minutes of trading after the appraisal deadline, paying more than the merger price and accepting an immediate ~$40 million paper loss to position himself to control the litigation.
  • Endeavor and Silver Lake allege the investors failed required securities and antitrust disclosures and coordinated share purchases to suppress prices paid. The investors dispute the allegations.
  • Icahn's attorney Christine Mackintosh called the new suit "procedurally bizarre" in a September 24 letter, noting Endeavor could have amended its existing answer instead.
  • For Silver Lake this is a rematch: it fought Icahn over the 2013 Dell buyout, a case that led Delaware's Supreme Court to require greater weight for negotiated deal prices in appraisal disputes.
  • Discovery in the related cases has drawn in Endeavor's advisor Centerview Partners and Netflix, whose $5 billion, 10-year deal for WWE's Monday Night Raw underscored TKO's value; WWE's Vince McMahon has been subpoenaed.

A Filmmaker Pitched Fox Five Meetings in One, Using AI Budget Math to Do It
FoxNXT chief Jon Flynn says a creative pitched Fox Entertainment a feature using AI tools to rationalize roughly 15% of the budget, then proposed reinvesting those savings into two additional shoot locations, all in one meeting.
Speaking at TheWrap's first AI Creator Day, FoxNXT executive vice president Jon Flynn described an unnamed creative's pitch that combined what would normally be five separate meetings into one, built entirely around AI-driven budget math: the standard budget for the feature, a roughly 15% reduction from AI tools, and a proposal to plow those savings back into production value rather than pocket them as savings. Flynn said this reflects a broader shift among pitching filmmakers, who increasingly frame proposals around AI-enabled cost reallocation (time saved, not just money saved) to fund more ambitious production choices within the same top-line budget.
Potential Talent Implication: As AI-driven savings become a line item studios expect in a pitch, the negotiating question shifts from whether AI is used to who controls the budget it frees up: production value on screen, or the fee and backend in the deal.
The Facts
  • Jon Flynn, EVP and head of FoxNXT (Fox Entertainment's internal AI/next-gen technology studio, launched in April), made the comments during a panel at TheWrap and What's Trending's first AI Creator Day, held Tuesday at UCLA's Ralph Freud Playhouse.
  • Flynn described an unnamed creative who came in with a standard budget figure, told Fox they wanted to use AI tools to "rationalize about 15% of the budget," and proposed reinvesting that 15% into two additional filming locations rather than cutting the top-line number.
  • Flynn said this wasn't a one-off: filmmakers are increasingly pitching with AI-driven budget consciousness built in from the start, including using AI to add effects like explosions or to recreate speculative footage (he cited TMZ's "Celebrity Crime Scene: Princess Diana" special) more cheaply than traditional methods.
  • Flynn, a former head of AI go-to-market strategy for media at Google, said the reframing that matters most is time, not cost: a 20% aggregated time/cost savings on a six-episode series could fund a sixth episode's worth of content within the same budget.

  • The panel, "Rewriting the Studio Model: Upskilling Talent for an AI-Powered Future," was moderated by TheWrap's Managing Editor for Business and PRO, Roger Cheng.

A Federal Judge Just Set Paramount's Theatrical Release Schedule Through 2031
A federal judge approved Paramount's $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery settlement Wednesday, locking in a 30-to-32-film annual quota, 45-day theatrical windows and a $30 million penalty per film missed; the deal closes October 6.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín entered a consent decree Wednesday settling Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery with the states and the WGA, clearing the last obstacle to a close expected October 6. The combined company must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for two years, then 32 for three more, with minimum wide and independent release counts and at least half produced or jointly produced by the combined studio; it must hold 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback. Missing the quota costs $30 million per film, with divestiture of Paramount's Miramax stake possible if the shortfall persists. Separately, the decree requires Paramount and Warner to keep basic-cable negotiations apart (violation risks forced divestiture of BET, VH1 and Comedy Central) and creates a five-member independent board, picked by Paramount, overseeing CBS News and CNN editorial standards. The same day, Paramount confirmed former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz will join as Co-CEO overseeing day-to-day operations and integration, starting October 6.
Potential Talent Implication: The settlement's 45-day theatrical window and per-film release quota now function as a court-enforced floor beneath any filmmaker's distribution negotiation with the combined studio, not merely a marketing promise the studio can quietly shorten.
The Facts
  • U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín entered a consent decree Wednesday, September 30, settling Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery with the state attorneys general and the WGA; the deal is expected to close October 6.
  • Combined company must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three years; must maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases; at least half of films must be produced or jointly produced by the combined company.
  • Must keep 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback for qualifying films.
  • A $30 million per-film penalty applies for missing the annual quota, with divestiture of Paramount's stake in Miramax in play if the shortfall remains unaddressed.
  • Paramount and Warner Bros. must keep basic-cable negotiations separate; a violation could trigger a forced divestiture of BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels. CNN and New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios.
  • The decree creates a five-member independent board, selected by Paramount, overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN.
  • The court declined a temporary restraining order sought by Paramount subscribers who alleged the deal would substantially reduce competition in streaming, news and theatrical distribution.
  • Paramount announced the same day that former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz will serve as Co-CEO of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros., starting October 6 and joining the board; Ellison remains Chairman/CEO focused on long-term strategy and creative direction while Kreiz focuses on day-to-day management and integration.
  • The approval follows Tuesday's announcement that Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is exiting, with HBO's Casey Bloys expected to take over the combined streaming business.

Paramount Gets the Warner Bros. Merger Without Selling a Thing
Paramount's $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger clears a 12-state settlement with no forced divestitures, a 45-day theatrical window, and CNN under an oversight board the Ellisons themselves will appoint.
Paramount and 12 state attorneys general settled the antitrust suit over its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, with California's Rob Bonta dropping demands for structural remedies like a CNN sale. The deal requires a five-person CNN/CBS News editorial board appointed by the Ellisons' own board, a $1.5 billion five-year U.S. production commitment, 30 films annually (rising to 32), a 45-day theatrical window, and no requirement to keep headquarters in California. Court approval from Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín is still pending; New Jersey Senator Cory Booker filed a letter opposing the settlement, which Paramount and the states rejected Monday.
Potential Talent Implication: A single Ellison-run studio releasing up to 32 films a year gives talent one fewer real bidder in the U.S. market, and the settlement's rental-term protections for theaters expire after three years.
The Facts
  • Deal value: $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance.
  • Settlement parties: 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta.
  • No forced divestitures (CNN, Miramax, BET remain with the combined company); a $30 million fine per film under the 30-film annual threshold, and a Miramax divestiture, are the sole breach remedies.
  • Combined company releases at least 30 films/year for two years, then 32/year after; 20% of the slate must carry a budget of $50M+; four films per year must qualify as "independent" (originated outside the combined entity, Disney, Universal or Sony, or based on an original screenplay).
  • Theatrical window: 45 days before PVOD/SVOD; 90 days to Paramount+/SVOD.
  • Rental-term protections (no cost increase to exhibitors) hold for years 1-3 only; the protection lapses in years 4-5, when the combined studio is expected to control roughly 30% of the box office.
  • David Ellison becomes sole CEO of both studios; the studios must negotiate TV network carriage deals separately.
  • WBD shareholders receive $31/share, all cash; deal expected to close October 2026.
  • Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) filed a letter opposing the settlement September 24; Paramount, WBD, and the 12 settling states filed a joint response September 28 calling the objection unpersuasive.

Pedro Pina, YouTube's VP for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told the Iberseries & Platino Industria conference in Madrid that Curry Barker (Obsession) and Kane Parsons (Backrooms), both YouTubers who moved into feature filmmaking, prove online creators can succeed at the box office, and predicted more will follow them into Oscar and Emmy contention. Pina said industry fear of YouTube has been "100 percent our fault" for not explaining how the platform pays and protects content, and that traditional media companies are now uploading more to YouTube as a result.

[The creators of] Obsession and Backrooms... were YouTubers who decided to go into the box office [business] – and they were a tremendous success this year. And I would expect to see more and more of these examples [at] the Emmys and Oscars" in coming years.

Casey Bloys Wins the Race to Run the Combined WarnerMount Streamer
Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is exiting effective today, clearing the way for HBO CEO Casey Bloys to run the combined 200-million-subscriber streamer once the $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery deal closes.
Cindy Holland, who has run Paramount+ and Pluto TV since January 2025, told staff Tuesday that "David is optimizing for HBO stability," ceding the combined-streamer path to HBO Max CEO Casey Bloys. Ellison praised Holland's tenure (Paramount+ topped 81 million subscribers) but did not name a successor. Per Puck, Bloys won the role by refusing from the outset to report to Holland, and had lunched with Netflix's Ted Sarandos, signaling he had other options.
Potential Talent Implication: With one executive now positioned to control greenlight authority across the combined platform, insiders expect WarnerMount to overpay for packages to keep talent from walking once anticipated layoffs and the uncertain fate of film chiefs De Luca and Abdy unsettle both studios.
The Facts
  • Cindy Holland's last day is today (September 29, 2026); she joined Paramount as an advisor to David Ellison in January 2025 and took oversight of Paramount+ and Pluto TV after the Paramount-Skydance merger closed in 2025.
  • Under Holland, Paramount+ hit an all-time high of 81 million global subscribers (as of Q2), its best retention in service history, and double-digit growth in engagement and revenue.
  • HBO Max CEO Casey Bloys is expected to take over the combined streaming business once the Paramount-WBD merger closes; Ellison has said the plan is to merge HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform with over 200 million subscribers, timeline unclear.
  • Per Puck (Kim Masters): Bloys made clear from the start he would never report to Holland, and had lunch with Netflix's Ted Sarandos, signaling he could leave if not given control.
  • Per Puck: WBD insiders describe the mood as "doomsday," bracing for "thousands and thousands of layoffs" to move quickly given the combined company's debt load.
  • Per Puck: WBD film chiefs Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy face uncertain futures after a year with no film breaking $100 million domestically; speculation centers on whether Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg could be elevated to oversee both studios' film operations.
  • Per Puck: one Warners executive predicted WarnerMount will "overpay for packages" to retain talent as competitors circle; Abbott Elementary creator Quinta Brunson has already left WBD for Disney.
  • Paramount Skydance filed two press releases with its own Investor Relations site September 28: an extension of expiration dates on pending exchange/tender offers, and the launch of a new notes offering, both tied to financing the WBD acquisition.
  • A Paramount spokesperson declined to comment on Holland's successor.

Indie Film Buyers Have Money and Audiences. They Don't Have Enough Movies.
Top agents at CAA, UTA, WME, Gersh and 30West say a record $4.7 billion summer box office has buyers hungry for independent films, but rising costs mean there aren't enough movies to sell them.
CAA's Roeg Sutherland estimates 70% of movies in the marketplace are now independently financed even when they carry a studio logo, and buyers are competing for bespoke, festival-style films earlier than ever. Rising below-the-line costs like transport have made U.S. production prohibitively expensive, and the domestic pay-TV market that once gave indies a second life has withered. A new federal bill, introduced September 24, would create a transferable tax credit of 20-30% on labor costs, stackable with state incentives. The Paramount-WBD merger is expected to leave only one of two new specialty labels, Warners' Clockwork or Paramount's Republic Pictures, standing.
Potential Talent Implication: Agents say the fight to lower guaranteed up-front talent fees in favor of performance-based pay has quieted because both sides increasingly agree that just getting the movie made matters more, shifting real leverage in specialty film deals toward structures that pay out on results.
The Facts
  • Summer 2026 box office hit a record $4.7 billion.
  • CAA's Roeg Sutherland: "I would say that 70 percent of the movies in the marketplace are independent, in one form or another... most things right now are being financed by outside money," even when a studio logo appears on the release.
  • Curry Barker's "Obsession," bought by Focus Features out of TIFF for $15 million, went on to gross $519 million globally, the highest-grossing festival acquisition of all time.
  • Olivia Wilde's "The Invite" sold to A24 for a reported $12 million in a Sundance bidding war and grossed $60 million worldwide; Lance Oppenheim's Robert Pattinson-led "Primetime" opened to just above $19 million domestically on a $15 million budget.
  • The Motion Picture Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced September 24 in the House and Senate, would create a transferable federal tax credit on labor costs (including above-the-line talent) starting at 20%, rising to 30% for indie projects and rural/disaster-zone shoots; stackable with state incentives; $1 million minimum spend.
  • WME's Deb McIntosh argues studios/streamers benefiting from the tax credit should be required to spend a share of content budgets licensing independently produced third-party film and TV to rebuild the post-theatrical secondary licensing market.
  • Paramount-WBD merger settlement commits the combined studio to $5 million annually for an independent-film acquisition fund and four theatrical releases per year of qualifying independent films (5-year term); one dealmaker called the commitment "ridiculous," saying: "I don't blame Paramount. I blame whoever thought this was a useful win for us."
  • The merger is expected to leave one of two new studio-funded specialty labels standing: Warners' Clockwork (led by former Neon CMO Christian Parkes) has acquired Sean Baker's "Ti Amo!," Park Chan-wook's "The Brigands of Rattlecreek" (Matthew McConaughey, Pedro Pascal, Austin Butler, Tang Wei) and "Nasty" (Mary Bronstein/Rose Byrne); Noah Baumbach left Netflix for a first-look deal at Warners under the Clockwork banner.
  • Paramount's Republic Pictures, led by Lia Buman, bought StudioCanal's "The Midnight Library" (Florence Pugh) out of Cannes for $36 million.

David Fincher Won't Renew His Netflix Deal, Joining a Growing Exit List
David Fincher will not renew his overall deal with Netflix when it expires next year, ending a 13-year run that began with "House of Cards" and continued through "Mindhunter," "Mank" and "The Killer."
Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw reports Fincher has decided against renewing his exclusive Netflix deal, signed in 2020, after directing three films for the service, including the upcoming $200 million "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," opening in IMAX November 25. Per Bloomberg, Fincher is not jumping to a rival studio and his next project could still land at Netflix; he simply does not want another big overall deal right now. The move follows Netflix shelving his "Squid Game: America" spinoff, and puts other Fincher-Netflix projects in question, including a "Chinatown" prequel series and the neo-western "Bitterroot."
Potential Talent Implication: An exclusive overall deal now looks like a constraint rather than a prize even for a filmmaker who once called Netflix the best place in Hollywood to work, suggesting top-tier directors increasingly value project-by-project freedom to chase theatrical over the security of a single-studio arrangement.
The Facts
  • Fincher's current Netflix deal, signed in 2020, expires in 2027; he will not renew it, per Bloomberg.
  • His Netflix filmography/TV work: directed and executive produced the first episode of "House of Cards" (2013), "Mindhunter," "Mank," "The Killer," and the upcoming "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" (Quentin Tarantino script, Brad Pitt starring, ~$200 million budget, IMAX release November 25, 2026).
  • Netflix shelved a planned U.S. "Squid Game" spinoff earlier (reported August 2026) as the company's franchise priorities shifted, not Fincher's decision, per prior reporting.
  • Projects now in question following the non-renewal: a Robert Towne-scripted "Chinatown" prequel series and the neo-western "Bitterroot," both previously in development at Netflix; a potential "Mindhunter" season 3 revival.
  • Bloomberg reports Fincher is not moving to a rival studio and could still make his next film at Netflix on a project-by-project basis; he is avoiding another exclusive overall commitment.
  • No on-the-record comment from Fincher, his reps, or Netflix is cited in any version of this story; sourcing rests on Bloomberg's own reporting without a named quote.

Paramount Markets $44.4 Billion in Debt to Close Its Warner Bros. Discovery Takeover
Paramount began marketing a $44.4 billion debt offering Monday, split between investment-grade and junk bonds, to fund its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition while a federal judge still withholds settlement approval.
Paramount is marketing $44.4 billion in debt, about $32 billion investment-grade and the equivalent of $12.4 billion in high-yield bonds, to help fund its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Bank of America and Citigroup hosted calls Monday and racked up enough demand to cover the offering the same day. The deal's last hurdle is a federal judge's approval of a settlement with 12 state attorneys general; she declined to sign off at a September 24 hearing and instead set a briefing schedule. Total cash consideration to WBD shareholders would run about $78 billion, and the combined company would carry over $80 billion in long-term debt, pushing annual interest expense above $6 billion.

Spanish and Portuguese Book Adaptations Draw Three Times the Demand of Original Series
Parrot Analytics says global demand for Spanish and Portuguese series rose 25% in two years, with South Korea up 243%, and credits The Eternaut with 230,000 new Netflix sign-ups.
Parrot Analytics, writing in TheWrap, reports that global audience demand for Spanish- and Portuguese-language series rose 25% between 2024 and September 2026, led by markets outside Latin America: South Korea (+243%), Japan (+148%) and China (+119%), with Turkish and Nordic demand also rising. Literary adaptations in those languages drew three times the global demand of non-IP original series this year. A New Bill Would Let Rights Owners Get Foreign Piracy Sites Blocked in the U.S.
The bipartisan DEFEND IP Act lets content owners ask a judge to designate a foreign piracy site and order U.S. internet providers to block it; AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox and Verizon oppose it.
House and Senate sponsors from both parties introduced the DEFEND IP Act on Sept. 24. A judge would decide whether a foreign site has "no commercially significant purpose" other than copyright violation; content owners could then seek an order directing U.S. internet providers to take "reasonable measures" to block it, renewable after 360 days, including for pirated live-event streams. It is the industry's first major site-blocking push since SOPA collapsed nearly 15 years ago. The Common Sense Copyright Coalition, whose members include Comcast, opposes it, citing the Supreme Court's March ruling in Cox v. Sony.
Potential Talent Implication: The order goes to whoever owns the copyright, so creators who hold their own rights would gain a direct remedy against foreign piracy, while talent paid on a studio's backend would depend on the studio choosing to use it.
The Facts
  • Bill: Deterring Extraterritorial Foreign Exploitation of Networks Damaging Intellectual Property (DEFEND IP) Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Sponsors: Reps. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), Ben Cline (R-VA); Sens. Thom Tillis (R-NC), Chris Coons (D-DE), Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Adam Schiff (D-CA).
  • Mechanism: a judge designates a "foreign digital piracy site" (one with "no commercially significant purpose or use other than committing a violation of copyright"); the order is subject to renewal after 360 days. Content owners may then seek an order directing service providers to "take reasonable measures to prevent users in the United States" from accessing it.
  • Covers transmission of live events from foreign locations that violate copyright.
  • Applicants must show they are "likely to suffer irreparable harm"; measures must be "technically feasible and effective" and not interfere with lawful content.
  • No mandated technical method; legal immunity for ISPs; applies to large-scale foreign sites.
  • Site-blocking is in use in almost 60 countries, per supporters.
  • Opposition: Common Sense Copyright Coalition (AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox, Verizon), citing new burdens on broadband providers and Cox v. Sony (March 2026: an ISP is not liable "for merely providing a service to the general public with knowledge that it will be used by some to infringe copyrights").
  • Lofgren: foreign piracy operations "exploit a loophole in our law."

Sony and Universal Music Group, the two majors that never licensed to Suno, sued again, claiming its new v6 model inherits infringement through user outputs and distillation from earlier models.
Sony Music and Universal Music Group filed another lawsuit against AI music company Suno, The Verge reported Sept. 25. The complaint says Suno's v6 model still infringes because it was trained on user outputs from earlier models built on unlicensed recordings, which it calls "model laundering." Sony also alleges distillation (training a new model to reproduce an older model's results). Suno said v6 was trained on partner-licensed content, user creations and preference signals. Sony and UMG are the holdouts that did not sign licensing deals with Suno.
Potential Talent Implication: If "model laundering" holds, a rights holder's claim follows the work into every later model built from it, which makes a license's reach over successor models and synthetic outputs worth as much as the first training fee.
The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: Sony and Universal Music Group; defendant: Suno. Complaint shared with The Verge.
  • Claim: v6 is trained on user outputs of prior models, which were trained on unlicensed music "ripped from YouTube and other sources."
  • Complaint: "Training a 'new' model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement; it launders it [...] V6 is not a fresh start; it is the fruit of the same poisoned tree."
  • Complaint: "even a model not directly trained on Plaintiffs' recordings is informed by, and benefits from, Suno's retained unauthorized copies."
  • Sony further alleges v6 was trained by distillation from earlier "teacher" models.
  • Suno (Rachel Racusen): "v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team." Suno did not specify whether that included uploaded audio.
  • Sony and UMG "are notable holdouts who did not sign a licensing agreement with Suno."
  • Related (The Verge, Sept. 15): UMG is suing DistroKid for alleged deceptive trade practices and copyright infringement.

The Federal Film Credit Bill Counts Star Salaries Toward the 20 Percent
Sens. Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and four House members introduced a 20% federal credit on U.S. production compensation Thursday, above-the-line salaries included, with 5% uplifts that can reach 30%.
A bipartisan group introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act on Thursday. It pays a 20% credit on compensation tied to a production, excluding residuals, and TheWrap reports that above-the-line salaries count, as they do in the UK and Canada. Uplifts of 5% each, to a 30% ceiling, go to shoots in rural opportunity zones or federal disaster areas (Los Angeles County qualifies until 2030), independent productions, shoots across 10 or more states, and studios that raise domestic output. Credits stack on state incentives. Congress is out until after the midterms; Schiff is aiming for the lame-duck session.
Potential Talent Implication: If the bill passes, a producer earns back 20 percent of star and director salaries, and up to 30 percent on an independent shot in Los Angeles, the same above-the-line credit that sent Barbie and Deadpool & Wolverine to shoot abroad.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Co-sponsors: Sens. Tim Scott (R-SC), Adam Schiff (D-CA); Reps. Linda Sanchez (D-CA), Brian Jack (R-GA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Laura Friedman (D-CA). Other backers: Reps. Judy Chu, David Kustoff, Mike Carey, Tom Suozzi.
  • Base rate: 20% of compensation directly related to a production, excluding residuals (Deadline). TheWrap: above-the-line talent salaries count toward the base.
  • Uplifts (5% each, 30% maximum, per TheWrap): at least 30% of principal photography days in a rural qualified opportunity zone or federally declared disaster area; independent production; at least 50% of principal photography and $10M in qualified compensation across 10 or more states; studio increases domestic productions relative to a historical foreign base amount.
  • L.A. County was declared a federal disaster area in 2025 after the Palisades and Altadena fires and keeps the designation until 2030 (TheWrap).
  • Eligibility: total cost above $1M; 75% of production in the U.S.; post-production and VFX covered; animation covered (TheWrap). Excluded: news, live sports, talk shows, daytime dramas, social media content, advertising, corporate video.
  • Credits transferable; stack on top of state incentives (31 states have them, per TheWrap).
  • Timing: House in recess through the midterms; Schiff said the plan is to pass it in the lame-duck session, possibly attached to a major funding bill. TheWrap: bill would take effect for productions at the start of 2027.
  • TheWrap: the $1M floor excludes microbudget films like Obsession (reported $750,000 budget, more than $500M global).
  • MPA statement: passage "could inject $250 billion into the country's economy and deliver nearly 145,000 new jobs every year."
  • Christopher Nolan (DGA president): "the most significant legislative effort in a generation to promote domestic film and television production."
  • Schiff credited Trump for the momentum and said he worked with the White House, Jon Voight and Spencer Pratt.

At a virtual hearing Thursday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín did not approve the consent decree (a court-enforced settlement) between Paramount and 12 state attorneys general. She asked whether it answers the states' Clayton Act claims and ordered replies to Booker's call for a public-interest review by noon PT Monday, Sept. 28. From Oct. 1, Paramount owes Warner Bros. Discovery about $7 million a day. The decree requires 30 theatrical releases in the first two years, 32 a year after that, a 45-day window, and a Miramax sale if output falls short.
Potential Talent Implication: The 30-film floor and 45-day window exist only once this judge signs, and the penalty for missing the output minimum is a forced sale of Miramax, which Paramount's lawyer told the court the company does not want to lose.
The Facts
  • Hearing: Thursday, Sept. 24, virtual, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín; ruling "in due course," no date given.
  • Judge: "The court isn't a rubber stamp of your agreement... I have some questions." Wants to "shore up the idea that this is not something that was the result of collusion, but instead was more of an arm's length process."
  • Homework: replies to Sen. Cory Booker's letter (asking for an independent public-interest review) due noon PT Monday, Sept. 28. Amicus briefs due 12:01 a.m. PT Sept. 25.
  • Booker: the settlement reached the court "without a competitive impact statement, without a public comment period, and without any formal opportunity for theaters, distributors, workers, or consumers to be heard." Paramount called his filing an "improper pseudo-amicus submission."
  • California Senior Assistant AG Paula Blizzard: "If we block the merger, it would be forever." Said states were prepared to go to trial March 2, 2027 if the decree is not approved (Deadline). Called relocation talk "blackmailing"; Paramount counsel Josh Holian (Latham & Watkins): "It's not blackmail. It's not a threat."
  • Miramax: divestiture required if output minimums are missed. Holian: "It's important IP. It's an important studio for us. We do not want to divest it." Cited Scary Movie 6 as a Miramax title in the 2026 domestic top 20.
  • Cable divestiture backstop: several BET channels, VH1, Comedy Central, Smithsonian, Destination America, Science.
  • Settlement terms (per Variety): no sale of the Paramount or Warner Bros. lots for five years; at least $300M a year additional U.S. film production ($1.5B over five years); at least 30 theatrical releases in the first two years and 32 in years 3-5; 45-day window for wide releases; news editorial independence board for CNN and CBS News; term runs through Dec. 31, 2031 if the deal closes this year.
  • Ticking fee: about $7M per day payable to WBD from Oct. 1.
  • Ellison memo: expected close in about two weeks if the settlement is approved in a timely fashion.
  • Same day: Paramount launched a $7.5B incremental Term B loan; plans about $44.4B of additional secured debt.

Paramount's Four-Indie-Films Pledge Counts Any Original Screenplay

Paramount's settlement with 12 states requires at least four independent films a year, but the consent decree defines an independent film as any movie based on an original screenplay or simply co-produced by Paramount, TheWrap reported in an analysis Wednesday. The Warner Bros. Discovery deal, expected to close in about two weeks, also requires 30 theatrical films a year for two years and 32 for the three after, with a $30 million penalty per missed film. Experts quoted called the penalties toothless. Paramount already holds overall deals with Jon M. Chu, the Duffer Brothers and James Mangold.

  • Output terms: at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years, 32 a year for the next three; at least four a year must be independent films; at least 20% must be blockbusters.
  • Definition: the consent decree defines independent films as movies "based on an original screenplay" or simply co-produced by Paramount (TheWrap's reading).
  • Penalties: $30 million per film that misses the theatrical goal; forced divestiture of the 49% Miramax stake within 12 months, and of BET, Comedy Central, VH1, Smithsonian, Destination America and Science Channel within 120 days, for other breaches.

The Paramount Settlement Fixes a 45-Day Theatrical Window for Five Years
Thirty films a year for two years, then 32, at least four of them independent, and $30 million per missed film goes into the Hollywood guilds' health and retirement plans.
Paramount Skydance settled the antitrust suit brought by 12 state attorneys general on Monday, clearing the last obstacle to its $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery. The proposed consent decree runs five years and, alongside the release commitments, guarantees a 45-day theatrical window with no streaming release before 90 days. No divestiture is required to close. Antitrust expert Matt Stoller told The Ankler that half the films need only be co-produced. Jane Fonda, reading the agreement, said a force majeure clause voids its terms in a strike, labor disruption or recession.
Potential Talent Implication: Paramount now owes a 45-day theatrical window for five years, which gives release bonuses, first-cycle backend and every term defined by a theatrical run a fixed number to point at instead of a negotiation.
The Facts
  • The suit was brought by 12 state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, against Paramount Skydance's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Settlement announced Monday, September 21, at a Bonta press conference.
  • Film commitments, quoting the proposed consent decree via THR: minimum 30 films per year for the first two years, rising to 32 per year for the following three. At least 20 (later 21) must be wide releases. At least four must be independent films. At least 20 percent must carry budgets over $50 million.
  • Windowing: a guaranteed 45-day theatrical window, with no SVOD window until at least 90 days.
  • Production spend: at least $300 million more annually on U.S. film production than was spent in 2025, or $1.5 billion across the agreement. Plus commitments on pricing to theaters.
  • Breach remedies on the film commitment: forced divestiture of Paramount's stake in Miramax, and $30 million per film short contributed to the healthcare and retirement plans of the major Hollywood guilds.
  • Lots: the combined entity may not sell or close the Paramount or Warner Bros. lots during the commitment period, and must use commercially reasonable efforts to operate them consistent with past practice, including leasing to third parties.
  • Cable: separate negotiation of basic cable carriage for five years, restrictions on affiliate fee changes, and a bar on using one defendant's confidential information in the other's affiliate negotiations. No cable divestitures required; a court can order divestiture on breach.
  • News: a five-member News Editorial Independence Board, named by Paramount's board of directors, each member a journalist of at least ten years' practice, with no more than two affiliated with the same political party.
  • Matt Stoller, to The Ankler: "Half of those have to be at least co-produced by Warnermount. So they don't have to make more than 15 or 16 films, and even those, they could just co-produce them. So the actual commitment is fewer films than they make now, for both studios combined."
  • Stoller on the force majeure provision: it includes an economic recession or labor strikes, so "if they do something that causes a strike or labor disruption of some sort, it says here that's beyond their control."
  • Jane Fonda, in a statement reported by TheWrap: the settlement "has a 'Force Majeure' clause stating that all its terms are void if there is a strike, labor disruptions, or an economic recession, meaning this settlement is also a union-buster."
  • Per Puck: Ellison met privately with New York AG Letitia James in Los Angeles on Friday, then met Bonta in the Bay Area; Bonta would not sign off unless the major Hollywood unions were on board, and Ellison spent the weekend calling guild heads.
  • Connecticut AG William Tong: "Connecticut wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News... I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more."
  • The Writers Guild of America settled its own suit blocking the merger on Monday, saying it continues to believe the merger will damage writers and the industry, but as a nonprofit could not afford to proceed alone.

David Zaslav told staff the deal closes no later than early October. The combined company carries roughly $80 billion in debt, and a county study put job losses at 4,500 over three years.
David Ellison has pledged $6 billion in cost savings from the Warner Bros. Discovery purchase, three times the target attached to Skydance's Paramount deal, which cut 2,600 jobs, or 15 percent of the workforce. The Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation estimated in August that the merger would cost 4,500 film and television jobs over three years. Abbott Elementary co-creator Quinta Brunson has already left Warner Bros. Television for Disney, and The Ankler reports at least one more showrunner is considering leaving. Paramount+ and HBO Max together have 220 million subscribers, per FlixPatrol.

The Facts
  • Zaslav wrote in a memo to employees, reviewed by The Ankler, that he expects the deal to close "no later than early October."
  • Ellison has pledged $6 billion in cost savings on the WBD acquisition. Skydance's $8 billion Paramount acquisition carried a $2 billion synergy target and produced 2,600 job cuts, 15 percent of the workforce and about 600 more than originally envisioned.
  • Disney's $71.3 billion Fox deal, closed in 2019, promised $2 billion in cost savings and was followed by roughly 4,000 job cuts.
  • The L.A. County Economic Development Corporation reported in August that the merger would cause 4,500 film and television job losses over three years.
  • Paramount is expected to carry roughly $80 billion in debt when the deal closes.
  • The settlement does not require Ellison to sell any of the 50 cable networks he stands to own. The single cable safeguard is a five-year term on affiliate dealmaking requiring distributors to negotiate separately for Paramount and WBD networks.
  • Executive overlap on close: Cindy Holland has overseen Paramount's entire streaming operation for the past year, with Jane Wiseman as head of originals at Paramount+. Arriving from WBD are Casey Bloys (HBO and HBO Max content), JB Perrette (global streaming CEO) and Channing Dungey (Warner Bros. Television Group and WBD U.S. networks). Sources told The Ankler that Bloys had no intention of reporting to Holland; one floated solution is a direct reporting line to Ellison.
  • Three TV studio operations would sit under one owner: Dungey's Warner Bros. Television, David Stapf's CBS Studios and Matt Thunell's Paramount Television Studios. After the Fox deal, Disney folded nearly all of its TV studio operations into 20th Television.
  • Quinta Brunson left Warner Bros. Television for Disney. The Ankler attributes the decision to uncertainty over who would run WBTV and to Ellison's Trump-friendly posture.
  • Licensing exposure: Paramount licensed 20 of its shows to Netflix in January; WBD licensed 15 to 20 titles to Netflix in October. After the Fox deal, Disney clawed back library titles from third-party streamers as agreements expired.
  • Mike Schur, creator of The Good Place, on Monday: "By the time this merger ruins HBO, destroys WB, gets 5,000 people fired, moves production overseas, and guts the quality of the movies the new studio makes, most people will have forgotten how fast the AGs caved and how little they got in this deal. Writers will not."
  • Per Puck, WBD shareholders receive $31 a share. The arbitrage spread on the deal had been as wide as 20 percent over the summer.

Penalties for shortfall include potential divestiture. Microsoft's Own Documents Call AI Training a Theft of Labor
A 2023 internal Microsoft document called model training "an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions," and OpenAI president Greg Brockman answered "Ah nice" when told of a hack to get around the New York Times paywall.
Court documents unsealed Thursday in the suit brought by The New York Times and eleven other publishers against Microsoft and OpenAI show executives weighing whether their systems were built on stolen content. Microsoft director of applied science Brent Hecht called the ingestion of copyrighted works potentially "the largest theft of labor in human history." Nick Turley, OpenAI's head of ChatGPT, said "our products are largely substitutive, period." Internal Microsoft data shows the Times losing 87 to 93 percent of clicks through Bing Chat. The Facts
  • Documents unsealed Thursday, Sept. 17, in the litigation by The New York Times and eleven other publishers against Microsoft and OpenAI.
  • 2023 internal Microsoft document: "Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models 'hoovering up' all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions," noting that "almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use."
  • Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht described the ingestion of copyrighted works as "an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions" and potentially "the largest theft of labor in human history." Hecht also said a win on the copyright defense would "make a complete mockery of the idea of fair use."
  • An OpenAI engineer told president Greg Brockman of a "hack to get around [the] nytimes paywall" as the company explored scraping the site. Brockman: "Ah nice." Publishers argue employees were instructed to devise strategies to circumvent paywalls "without detection."
  • Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that "anything that is paywalled should be licensed by anyone who wants to use it," and said that had he known OpenAI scraped restricted content he would have "invoked" Microsoft's right to require retraining of the models.
  • Fair use is a four-factor test; OpenAI and Microsoft bear the burden. Supreme Court precedent holds that an "evasive motive" and violations of industry ethical standards undercut a fair use defense.
  • Fourth factor, market effect: Bing Chat copied all but two of the first 396 words of the Times's 2023 article "The Secrets Hamas knew about Israel's Military." An exhibit shows 100 other instances of GPT memorizing Times articles with word-for-word copying.
  • Internal Microsoft data: Times click-through rates fell 87 to 93 percent when users searched through Bing Chat rather than traditional web search.
  • Publishers argue Microsoft and OpenAI cannot claim no licensing market exists when they have signed deals with other publishers.

Private Equity Is Buying Literary Estates the Way It Bought Song Catalogs

Two investment-backed buyers are assembling literary estates as an asset class. International Literary Properties, fully funded by Connecticut firm Viking Global, holds Tennessee Williams, Paddy Chayefsky, Langston Hughes, Evelyn Waugh and Ellen Raskin, and borrowed $100 million from Fifth Third Bank in January. Atticus Works launched this summer with $100 million from Primary Wave. Estates are selling at eight to 12 times annual royalties, against about 17 times for music catalogs, per Citrin Cooperman. ILP has Tennessee Williams productions set for New York and London and a Westing Game feature in development with a major studio.
