The Facts
  • International Literary Properties launched in 2019, is now fully funded by Viking Global, and holds or manages estates including Tennessee Williams, Paddy Chayefsky, Langston Hughes, Evelyn Waugh, Ngaio Marsh, James Cain, Eric Ambler, Ed Emberley and Ellen Raskin. In Hughes and Chayefsky it owns a significant stake and manages.
  • ILP borrowed $100 million from Fifth Third Bank in January. CEO Michael Barra: "You know an asset class is maturing when a bank will offer you bank debt."
  • Atticus Works, founded this summer by investor and author Richard Hurowitz, launched with $100 million from Primary Wave, the private-equity-backed music publisher behind early catalog deals for Hall & Oates, Smokey Robinson, Kurt Cobain and Def Leppard. No acquisitions announced yet.
  • Precedent corporate deals: Netflix bought the Roald Dahl estate in 2021 for a reported $700 million; Embracer paid nearly $400 million for a piece of J.R.R. Tolkien rights.
  • Multiples: literary estates fetching eight to 12 times annual royalties; music catalogs peaked near 30 times for artists like Bruce Springsteen in the early 2020s and have settled around 17, per Citrin Cooperman. Jeffrey Archer, 86, has declined repeated offers at eight to 12 times, per his son James: "Guess we value them higher than the market."
  • Tax logic for sellers: converts royalty income taxed as ordinary income into a capital gain, and turns an illiquid asset into something an estate can divide.
  • Targets: deep backlists already generating revenue, from dead writers' estates, living writers near the end of a career, or mid-career authors simplifying. New books are out of scope. Buyers want 100 percent or close to it. About two-thirds of Big Five book sales are backlist, per Publishers Weekly.
  • Primary Wave CEO Larry Mestel: "We're only interested in one particular area of the business, which is the icon and legend business... Either the songs have to be iconic or the artists have to be legendary for us to buy the assets."
  • Short stories are treated as inventory rather than ballast; Prime Video greenlit a Stephen King short-story limited series this summer and Netflix did the same for a Roald Dahl adult collection. Manager Scott Glassgold has sold unpublished short stories for high six- and low seven-figure options.
  • Non-monetary deal points cited: estates excluding industries such as gambling or tobacco; one 50-title estate held back a single book from screen development.
  • Counter-view from agents and managers: the number of meaningful estates is finite, most have been "picked over through the years," and revenue growth is harder than a pitch deck suggests.

Amazon, Apple, Sony and A24 Are the Last Four Holdouts on Producer Healthcare
Lionsgate Motion Picture Group, Neon and FilmNation agreed to cover producer healthcare and pay development fees at multiples of $25,000, a figure set in the early 1970s.

  • Not complied: Amazon MGM, Apple, Sony Pictures Entertainment, A24. None provided comment for the story. Last year Sony insiders told Variety the studio evaluates healthcare costs project by project; a source familiar with A24 said the company has provisions in place to address producer needs.
  • Healthcare mechanism: payment into the MPI Non-Affiliate Agreement for a period prior to principal photography, during shooting, and for select weeks of postproduction. Producers may instead elect equivalent reimbursement for another policy they maintain or prefer.

Variety reports producer profit participation has eroded in the streaming era.

A24 Claimed Worldwide Rights to a Property Anyone Is Free to Copy
The SCP Foundation Wiki says A24 and Spooky Pictures never contacted it, and that the CC BY-SA 3.0 license bars exclusivity, DRM and any exclusive streaming window.
A24 and Spooky Pictures announced V/H/S: SCP, set in the SCP Foundation universe, with Deadline reporting A24 held worldwide rights. The SCP Foundation Wiki, which hosts the source material, says it was never contacted and that the material carries a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 license, which permits commercial derivative works only if the derivative carries the same license. Under those terms the film could not ship with DRM (copy protection), could not be distributed exclusively, and could be streamed by any service without payment. The Wiki says that is why no Hollywood film has used SCP material before.
Potential Talent Implication: The license on the underlying material sets what a buyer can actually sell, and on open-licensed source there is no exclusivity to grant, no window to hold and no streaming fee to share.
The Facts
  • Project: V/H/S: SCP, a new installment of the V/H/S horror anthology set in the SCP Foundation universe, announced with A24 attached and Spooky Pictures producing. Deadline reported A24 holding "worldwide rights."
  • License: the SCP Foundation, all SCPs and related concepts are released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0. It permits commercial derivative works subject to the ShareAlike obligation: the derivative must itself be released under CC BY-SA 3.0 or later.
  • The Wiki's stated consequences if the film is a derivative work: no DRM or technological measures preventing copying; no distribution exclusivity, so any commercial streaming service could stream it without payment to anyone and anyone could upload it to YouTube; no ability to stop other parties making their own SCP works or derivatives of this film; no terms on theaters preventing them from making copies. Violating the license forfeits all rights to distribute any SCP-derived work.
  • Contact: "we have not had any communication with the filmmakers, producers, or distributors for this project, despite our best efforts, and to the best of our knowledge they have not made any efforts to contact us." Wiki admin DrEverettMann told The Verge: "We have made several attempts to contact them since the announcement of the project but haven't received a response."
  • The Wiki's stated ask: either release the film under CC BY-SA 3.0 or later and take no hostile action against license-compliant parties, or release it with no SCP-derived content. It states no preference between the two and says it is not seeking money: "We do not have the legal ability to do so, and would not even if we could."
  • Derivative-work scope: the Wiki says a film using no existing SCP anomalies would still be a derivative work, comparing it to new Star Trek series with new casts and ships.
  • Precedent: the Wiki states this license structure "is why, despite prior interest, no Hollywood films have been created using SCP material."
  • Statement page last edited September 15, 2026. SCP International, the common organization for all SCP language branches, issued a joint statement.
  • A24's Backrooms, also originating on 4chan, was made with the creator of a YouTube series popular in that community, per The Verge.

  • Unstated context, per Deadline: tensions across the Gulf from the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war, including retaliatory strikes on the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman; Iran's moves on the Strait of Hormuz; and a recent flareup in Saudi Arabia's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi group.

The UK Writers Guild President Wants Undeclared AI in a Script Treated as Fraud
Jack Thorne told the Writers' Guild of Great Britain that a studio should be able to sue a writer who delivers an AI-generated script without declaring it, and asked the BBC and Channel 4 to add their own sanctions.
Jack Thorne, who wrote Adolescence and serves as WGGB president, said in a speech titled Authorship in the Age of AI that executives and writers close to him describe writers using AI "to cheat." He drew the line at replacement rather than assistance: discussion, spellcheck and layout are fine, prompts in place of writing are not. "Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful," he said, and a studio that commissioned the script "should have the right to take me to court."
Potential Talent Implication: Thorne is asking for a rule that turns the authorship warranty in a writing agreement from boilerplate into a term a studio could sue on, and the line he draws between assistance and replacement is where that warranty would sit.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Jack Thorne, WGGB president, writer of Adolescence, Lord of the Flies and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. Speech titled Authorship in the Age of AI.
  • Thorne: "I have spoken to a number of execs and studio heads about their use of AI, and got hugely different responses, but what I did hear from them, and what anecdotally I've heard from a few writers close to me, is that some in my profession are using AI to cheat."
  • The distinction he draws: "What I'm not talking about here is using AI to help: To discuss things with, to check for spelling errors or help with layout. I'm talking about using AI as a replacement for endeavour, as a replacement for writing at all."
  • His proposed legal standard: "Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful. If you use AI to generate content and you do not declare it as such, then that is fraud and the companies you do it to should be entitled to prosecute you."
  • His worked example: "If I excitedly pitch my Mars show to Netflix and they send me to script, and I write the script using AI and do not tell them, then they should have the right to take me to court."

CBS Says Dropping a Writer Is Protected Creative Speech
John Lowe's Matlock deal guaranteed 20 weeks and then ran week to week at the studio's discretion, and CBS says the decision not to extend it shaped the scripts.
CBS Television Studios moved Friday to dismiss claims in writer John Lowe's suit under California's anti-SLAPP law, which allows early dismissal of claims that chill free speech. Lowe alleges a hostile work environment and retaliatory firing after he reported that a supervisor called Juneteenth "Coonteenth." CBS lawyer Adam Levin wrote that staffing judgments "are creative, because the composition of the room determines the content of the scripts that are shot for exhibition to the public." CBS says Lowe was never terminated: his deal guaranteed 20 weeks, then continued week to week.
Potential Talent Implication: The guaranteed-weeks term is the part of a staff writing deal a studio cannot recast as a creative judgment, and everything past it runs at the studio's discretion.
The Facts
  • CBS Television Studios filed the motion on Friday, September 11, under California's anti-SLAPP statute, seeking early dismissal of some claims.
  • Lowe alleges Matlock's showrunner and executive producers created a workplace "permeated by sexually explicit and discriminatory conduct," and that he was terminated after reporting the Juneteenth remark.
  • CBS argument, per outside counsel Adam Levin: "A writer who is performing well and having a positive impact on the scripts may be extended, while a writer who is not performing well is generally let go earlier. Those judgments are creative, because the composition of the room determines the content of the scripts that are shot for exhibition to the public."
  • Contract structure per the motion: 20 guaranteed weeks, then week to week at CBS's discretion. CBS says it declined to extend rather than terminated.
  • CBS detailed alleged performance issues: failure to follow writing assignments, outlines that did not incorporate notes or capture the show's tone, late arrivals to set and departures during shooting, all documented with human resources.
  • Executive producer Nicki Renna said in a declaration that flashbacks in a Lowe outline "did not work" and "another scene did not make sense."
  • Showrunner Jennie Snyder Urman said in a declaration that the "Coonteenth" claim was "made up" by Lowe.
  • CBS Studios statement: "confident that Lowe's accusations are demonstrably inaccurate and maliciously fabricated" and "we stand firmly behind our producers."

Disney Hired the Lawyer Who Papered Warner's Last Two Sales
Dan Weinberger spent 19 years at Warner Bros., worked the $108 billion AT&T sale and the $43 billion WarnerMedia-Discovery combination, and starts at Disney on September 28.
Disney has hired Dan Weinberger as deputy general counsel for corporate transactions, per an internal memo from corporate general counsel David Howard. Weinberger spent 19 years at Warner Bros., most recently as senior vice president of business and legal affairs, covering mergers and acquisitions, equity and debt investments, joint ventures and strategic partnerships. He played a key role in the $108 billion sale of Time Warner to AT&T and the $43 billion combination of WarnerMedia with Discovery, and led Warner's video game expansion and its China joint ventures including Tencent Video.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney is adding transaction lawyers while its nearest rival is being sold, and change-of-control and assignment clauses are the terms that decide whether a deal signed with one company survives its transfer to another.
The Facts
  • Role: deputy general counsel overseeing corporate transactions at Disney. Start date September 28, 2026.
  • The hire was announced in an internal memo from David Howard, Disney's general counsel for its corporate legal unit.
  • Weinberger is a 19-year Warner Bros. veteran, most recently senior vice president of business and legal affairs.
  • His remit at Warner covered mergers and acquisitions, equity and debt investments, joint ventures, strategic partnerships and general corporate transaction matters, advising C-suite leadership on deal structuring, negotiation strategy and deal execution across legal and business units.
  • Named achievements: a key role in the $108 billion sale of Time Warner to AT&T and the $43 billion combination of WarnerMedia with Discovery.
  • He also led the expansion of Warner's video game business and the formation of joint ventures in the Chinese entertainment market, including Tencent Video.
  • Education: J.D., UCLA School of Law; B.A., Stanford University.
  • Context: Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery is in front of a dozen state attorneys general, with court-ordered settlement talks set for late October.

The Facts

(the 'Merger') will enhance competition, not diminish it."

An R-Rated Original Just Beat Universal's Entire Franchise Library

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey becomes Universal's highest-grossing release ever this weekend at $1.684 billion worldwide, ahead of 2015's Jurassic World at $1.677 billion, with $601.2 million domestic and $1.083 billion international. Studios Stopped Developing and the Ideas Moved Outside
CAA's Roeg Sutherland told TIFF's new market that studios have stopped developing the way they used to and that the ideas directors and actors want are not coming through traditional routes.
At TIFF: The Market, CAA Co-Head of Media Finance Roeg Sutherland said studio development has contracted and that talent is hunting material outside the usual pipeline: "All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes." He said the market now resets every two weeks rather than every six months. FilmNation CEO Glen Basner said independent distributors package to reduce risk by pre-selling to streamers, which builds films for streaming rather than a theatrical proposition.
Potential Talent Implication: When studios stop developing, the person holding the underlying material sets the terms of the package, and the option and the attachment now carry the leverage the development deal used to.
The Facts
  • Panel at TIFF: The Market, the Toronto International Film Festival's new film and TV market, with TIFF's Geoff Macnaughton.
  • Roeg Sutherland, Co-Head of Media Finance, CAA: "It's cyclical, [but] what is happening now is that things are changing so much quicker than they ever have. Instead of having to reset yourself every six months, you have to reset yourself every two weeks."
  • Sutherland: "Things will be uncomfortable, but we work in independent film; everything's uncomfortable pretty much all the time."
  • Sutherland: "Studios are not developing the way they used to, which presents an unbelievable opportunity to the independent community. All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes."
  • Glen Basner, CEO, FilmNation Entertainment, on independent distributors: "This is my biggest complaint about the independent distribution community right now. There's a very traditional approach to packaging. They're worried about how much risk they're taking, and so they know they need to mitigate that by selling their movie to pay television, and specifically to streamers. The only problem is that we're [then] building movies for the streamer companies. That may work great on streaming, but it's not the same thing as building a theatrical proposition."
  • Basner: "We are trying to evolve to say, 'how do we make the best possible film so that it can compel people, in an undeniable way, to see it in a movie theater?' And if they do go and see it, then it's going to work in home video, it's going to work on pay TV, it's going to work on free television."
  • Basner on theatrical: "I think 2027 is going to be a great year at the theatrical box office."

Creators Are Selling Tools Around the Archive, Not Just the Newsletter
Two former Substack executives launched a consultancy arguing subscriptions are no longer enough, pointing to Lenny Rachitsky's $400-a-year tier bundling more than $30,000 of software discounts.
Puck reports that former Substack executives Austin Tedesco and Catherine Valentine have launched a consultancy, Spur, arguing that creator businesses need products beyond newsletters, podcasts and events as AI aggregation erodes search and social traffic. Tedesco said AI now makes personalized tools cheap enough for creators to build against their own archives. Lenny Rachitsky's Product Pass bundles roughly 25 software tools he valued at $25,000 in January and more than $30,000 now, for a tier costing $400 a year; his newsletter has about 1.2 million total subscribers. Patreon found 81 percent of creators want a direct channel to fans.

The Facts
  • Austin Tedesco and Catherine Valentine, two former Substack executives, are launching a consultancy called Spur. The news was broken by Emily Sundberg's Feed Me.

(Referring to a hypothetical bot serving The Ringer's Sean Fennessey's movie recommendations.)
  • Tedesco: "Let us build the tools to think about growth for you in what we think will be the highest-leverage way, not just the way that is generally recommended."
  • Tedesco on why creators default to known products: "You get into this hamster wheel and it's so hard to get off, because it takes a lot of resources, effort, time, and money."

Rachitsky has roughly 1.2 million total newsletter subscribers, with a smaller number on premium tiers. He has said the pass paid for itself for most subscribers after a couple of redemptions.

YouTube Is Showing NFL Games Without Buying NFL Rights
YouTube ingested Peacock Premium into YouTube Premium in late July, delivering a full NFL season including postseason, plus NBA, MLB and the Olympics, without licensing a single game from the league.

A Documentary That Names Its Abusers Is Harder to Sue
California's Second District Court of Appeal reversed the trial court on Thursday and dismissed Dan Schneider's defamation suit against Warner Bros. Discovery, Maxine Productions and Sony Pictures Television over Quiet on Set.
The panel found the docuseries "clearly distinguishes" between the gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior and sexual innuendo its participants attribute to Schneider and the child sexual abuse it attributes to three named individuals, and noted the series told viewers a Nickelodeon investigation found no evidence of abuse by him. A Los Angeles Superior Court judge had let the case proceed in 2024 after finding viewers could draw "damning implications." Schneider had sought damages and an order removing portions of the series or taking it down entirely. Gibson Dunn handled the appeal for Warner Bros.
Potential Talent Implication: A documentary that says plainly who did what is protected even where the editing invites a darker reading, which is what a filmmaker's insurer and its on-camera participants are relying on when they agree to name a living subject.
The Facts
  • California's Second District Court of Appeal ruled Thursday, September 10, reversing a 2024 decision by Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Ashfaq G. Chowdhury that had allowed the suit to proceed.
  • From the decision: "The documentary clearly distinguishes between the lamentable conduct that its participants attribute to Schneider, gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior, and inappropriate sexual innuendo, and the child sexual abuse explicitly attributed to three named individuals."
  • The court said it would "refrain from splitting hairs to find an allegation of child sexual abuse where the only such abuse discussed is explicitly attributed to named perpetrators and the documentary expressly states that an investigation into Schneider found no evidence of abuse."
  • Schneider had targeted the editing: episode two introduces abusers Brian Peck and Jason Handy while cutting to images of Schneider. The panel reviewed the segment and found roughly six minutes focused on Handy with no time given to Schneider in those scenes.
  • "Schneider's attempt to find an alternative meaning than what is expressly stated in the documentary is unavailing," the order stated.
  • Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV debuted in 2024 on Max and Investigation Discovery. In episode three, Drake Bell came forward as the anonymous victim in the case against dialogue coach Brian Peck, convicted in 2004.
  • Defendants named in the complaint: Warner Bros. Discovery, Maxine Productions and Sony Pictures Television.
  • Warners' appeal was handled by Theodore J. Boutrous, Ilissa Samplin, Zachary C. Freund and Connor S. Sullivan of Gibson Dunn. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and the International Documentary Association filed amicus briefs supporting the studio.
  • Schneider lawyer Gerry Silver said the producer is evaluating "options for further review and appeal."

Ten States Have Pulled Back the Tax Breaks They Gave Data Centers
New Jersey cancelled $250 million in AI and data center credits in August, Illinois suspended its program for two years from July 1, and the governors of Ohio and Texas moved against their own exemptions.
Newsweek counted action across ten states. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker suspended new data center incentives for two years beginning July 1, 2026, to study energy demand, water use and electricity costs. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine paused new applications in May. Texas Governor Greg Abbott recommended repealing sales tax exemptions in June, arguing developers should cover more power and infrastructure costs. Virginia kept its exemption but added a tax of $0.011 per kilowatt hour on data center electricity. Minnesota repealed its electricity exemption effective July 2025. Arizona, Georgia and Michigan have bills pending; Washington narrowed its exemptions through Senate Bill 6231.

The Facts
  • Newsweek, published September 9, 2026, documents action in Arizona, Georgia, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Ohio, Texas, Virginia and Washington.
  • New Jersey enacted the "End Data Center Tax Credits Act" in August 2026, eliminating the remaining $250 million available for AI and data center projects under the Next New Jersey Program.
  • Illinois: Governor JB Pritzker announced a two-year suspension of new data center incentives beginning July 1, 2026, to study energy demand, water use and electricity costs.
  • Ohio: Governor Mike DeWine paused new applications for the sales tax exemption in May 2026.
  • Texas: Governor Greg Abbott recommended repealing sales tax exemptions and other data center incentives in June 2026. No repeal has been enacted.
  • Virginia: Senator Danica Roem's proposed repeal (S.B. 30) projected roughly $1 billion in additional general fund revenue in year one and $1.1 billion in year two. It was not enacted; the 2026 budget compromise kept the exemption and added a $0.011 per kilowatt hour tax on data center electricity consumption.
  • Minnesota repealed the sales tax exemption for electricity used by qualified data centers, effective for purchases after June 30, 2025.
  • Washington's Senate Bill 6231 removed exemptions for replacement server equipment and ended eligibility for certain refurbished data centers, keeping incentives for qualifying new facilities.
  • Arizona Senate Bills 1463 and 1467 and House Bill 2820 would repeal the state's data center certification program. Georgia Senate Bill 410 would stop new exemption certificates. Michigan House Bills 5396 and 5398 target the sales tax exemption and property tax treatment. None has been enacted.
  • Newsweek reports the stated objections are electricity demand, water consumption, grid infrastructure costs and lost tax revenue, and that incentive programs have cost more than originally projected as AI demand grew. Newsweek says it contacted the Data Center Coalition for comment and was awaiting a response.

The Federal Film Credit Has Bill Language and No Time to Pass It

  • Bill name: the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, a Trump-coined title.
  • House sponsors: Linda Sanchez (D-CA, Ways and Means) and Laura Friedman (D-CA, ex-Rysher Entertainment, Schiff's successor in Burbank). Republicans Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and Brian Jack (R-GA) are also in the mix.

Trey Parker and Matt Stone's untitled musical, known inside Paramount as Whitney Springs, was picked up in January 2022 as a negative pickup, lost two release dates and came off the schedule entirely last November.
Paramount committed more than $100 million to an untitled Trey Parker and Matt Stone feature through a negative pickup, a deal where the studio buys a finished film and the filmmakers keep whatever is left of the budget, Matthew Frank reported in The Ankler. One person familiar put the total at $150 million; another put it between $70 and $80 million. Kendrick Lamar and Dave Free produce and Lamar wrote original, unreleased songs. Paramount dated the picture for July 4, 2025, moved it to March 20, 2026, then took it off the schedule last November.
Potential Talent Implication: A negative pickup pays the filmmakers at delivery and lets them keep what they did not spend, so Parker and Stone have their nine-figure money while the picture sits undated and every part of a deal that pays on release stays unpaid.
The Facts
  • Project: untitled feature written by South Park veteran Vernon Chatman, directed by Trey Parker, produced by Matt Stone, Kendrick Lamar and Dave Free. Known internally at Paramount as Whitney Springs. Parker plays the town's mayor.
  • Premise: a musical comedy about reparations for slavery, set at a historical slave plantation museum in the Midwest, following a young Black re-enactor who clashes with the town's racist mayor.
  • Deal: "Paramount committed more than $100 million to the project through a negative pickup - where the creators keep what is left from the budget." One source put the total cost at $150 million; another put the deal terms between $70 and $80 million.
  • The budget was defrayed across multiple Paramount divisions, including Chris McCarthy's cable group. The film has no A-list cast or heavy visual effects; "whatever the filmmakers didn't spend, they kept."
  • Timeline: Paramount execs read the script at Park County in late 2021; the studio picked it up in January 2022. Then-Paramount Pictures head Brian Robbins called it "one of the funniest and most original scripts we've ever read" at CinemaCon 2024. Set for July 4, 2025; moved in March 2025 to March 20, 2026; removed from the schedule in November 2025; unmentioned at David Ellison's first CinemaCon in April 2026.
  • Statement from Stone and Parker: "We take full responsibility for the schedule delay of this movie. We apologize to our partners at pgLang and Paramount and we appreciate their patience. South Park and life's circumstances have gotten in the way but we still believe in the project."

Creators Wrote Their Own AI Definitions Before the Studios Did
The Standards & Definitions Project launched Wednesday with a glossary of about 180 AI terms and a visualizer scoring roughly 150 creative jobs from 0 to 5 on AI replacement.
The Creators Coalition on AI, founded nine months ago by Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Daniel Kwan and late-night veteran Ted Tremper, launched a public Standards & Definitions Project on Wednesday. It carries a glossary of roughly 180 AI terms and an AI Impact Visualizer rating about 150 jobs across 11 creative areas, including directing, sound, animation, writing and acting, from 0 (does not touch the job) to 5 (could do the whole job). More than 250 people have been polled and most roles still read "required knowledge." Founders say the shared terms are meant for guild negotiations and individual talent deals.
Potential Talent Implication: Human-authored content and AI digital performance now have written definitions that did not come off a studio's paper, and those are the terms a deal about AI use will be argued in.
The Facts
  • Launch date: Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Project name: the Standards & Definitions Project, run by the Creators Coalition on AI (CCAI).
  • Glossary: approximately 180 AI terms.
  • AI Impact Visualizer: about 150 jobs across 11 creative areas, scored 0 to 5 on likelihood of AI role replacement. Many roles broken into dozens of sub-categories.
  • More than 250 people polled to date; the project targets responses in the thousands. Major updates planned quarterly. A survey page vets users to confirm they work in Hollywood.
  • CCAI founded December 2025 by Gordon-Levitt, Kwan, Ted Tremper and more than a dozen others. Thousands of signatories including Judd Apatow, Ava DuVernay, Margot Robbie, Guillermo del Toro and Hiro Murai. David Goyer is a founder and the group's secretary.
  • Two conventions were held this summer with guild-based delegates from all 11 areas; the most recent concluded ten days before launch.
  • Sample definition, human-authored content: "Creative work in which no generative AI system contributed expressive content, irrespective of the technological tools otherwise used in its creation, capture, processing, or distribution."
  • Sample definition, AI Digital Performance: "the application of artificial intelligence to capture, synthesize, modify, and/or replicate a human being or animal performer's natural person's human individual's performance attributes, which can include visual and physiological likeness, both still and kinetic facial expression, body movement, biometric characteristics, choreography, and voice whether partially or in full."
  • Tremper: "The purpose of these resources is take all the things we hear about with regard to AI and establish ground truth." He also cited a use case in drafting statehouse bills.
  • Gordon-Levitt: "Artists and content creators are a canary in the coal mine."
  • Kwan: "If we're going to be fighting for transparency, we should also be modeling it."

Imax Is Putting Up the Capital to Take a Bigger Share of the Box Office
Imax has passed $600 million in global box office this quarter against a previous best in the mid-$300 millions, and Rich Gelfond said The Odyssey is nearing $500 million in Imax receipts on about 1% of the world's screens.
Rich Gelfond told the Goldman Sachs Communacopia conference that Imax screens have passed $600 million in global box office receipts this quarter, against a best-ever quarter in the mid-$300 millions in 2023. Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is approaching $500 million in Imax receipts, more than double the $230 million Avatar drew on its initial run, on roughly 1% of the world's screens. Imax keeps about 18 cents of every box office dollar and has moved from licensing its technology toward a joint venture model where it supplies more of the capital for a larger share of the gross.

Channel 4 Is Cutting a Quarter of Its Staff to Protect the Programming Budget

Channel 4 will cut roughly 340 roles, 28 percent of its workforce, by the end of 2026.   • Dogra: "Today marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programs audiences love." The Draft Federal Film Credit Covers Star Pay, Not Just Crew
The base credit is 20 percent of all labor costs above and below the line, four optional uplifts of five percent each take it to 30, and it stacks on state incentives to 60 percent or more.
Reps. Nathaniel Moran and Linda Sanchez, both on House Ways and Means, are drafting a federal film and television incentive expected to be introduced this month. The base credit covers 20 percent of all labor costs, above the line as well as below. Producers can claim up to two of four five percent uplifts: rural opportunity zones, independent productions, repatriated filming, or $10 million spent across ten states. Reality TV and animation qualify, news and sports do not. Producers can sell the credit but cannot claim a refund.
Potential Talent Implication: A federal credit that covers above-the-line labor makes star, director and writer compensation a subsidized line in the budget rather than the line a studio cuts first to make a picture work in a cheaper territory.
The Facts
  • Base credit: 20 percent of all labor costs, both below-the-line and above-the-line.
  • Four uplifts of five percent each: filming in a rural opportunity zone; an independent production; bringing a certain amount of filming back to the U.S. from abroad; spending at least $10 million in ten different states in a year. Producers may claim up to two, for a maximum of 30 percent.
  • The federal credit stacks on state incentives, which supporters say could total 60 percent or more depending on location.
  • Eligible: films, scripted TV, reality TV and animation. Not eligible: news and sports broadcasts.
  • The credit can offset federal income tax or be sold to another taxpayer. It is not refundable.
  • Drafters: Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) and Rep. Linda Sanchez (D-Calif.), both on House Ways and Means. Rep. Laura Friedman (D-Calif.) and Rep. Brian Jack (R-Ga.) also working on it.
  • The bill is expected to be introduced this month, possibly by the end of next week.
  • Trump endorsed a federal incentive in a Truth Social post on August 31.
  • The draft broadly aligns with the Motion Picture Association's request. The MPA and entertainment unions have been advocating for a year.
  • A California proposal for a bonus in federally declared disaster zones, which would cover all of Los Angeles County after the 2025 fires, is not in the current draft.
  • The bill has not gone to the Joint Committee on Taxation for a cost score. Variety reports the cost will run into the billions.
  • Friedman: "I would be very happy for it to happen in the lame duck. I can't promise that's possible."
  • Friedman on Trump's involvement: "I can't tell you the number of texts that have come in from people who have offered to help."

Family Offices Put $22.2 Billion Into Media in Two Years
FINTRX counted 137 investments across 123 media and entertainment companies since 2024, from Access Industries' $827 million in DAZN to TWG Global's $10 billion for the Los Angeles Lakers.
TheWrap reported that family offices, the private firms managing assets for one family or a small group, have become a direct financing route into entertainment. FINTRX, a private wealth data platform, counted 137 investments across 123 media and entertainment portfolio companies over two years, worth $22.2 billion, plus 22 follow-on investments. Wealth advisor Kerry Finn of Sequoia Sentinel said checks often run $1 million to $5 million across multiple projects rather than one large commitment. Julie Zorn, head of CAA's Global Family Office Advisory, said families are building verticals in sports, entertainment and media.
Potential Talent Implication: Kerry Finn's clients are writing $1 million to $5 million checks across multiple projects and Julie Zorn says the families are building their own entertainment verticals, so the capital behind a talent-owned company now sits outside both the studios and the banks.
The Facts
  • FINTRX count over two years: 137 investments, 123 media and entertainment portfolio companies, $22.2 billion aggregate value, plus 22 follow-on investments.
  • Split by year: 37 in 2024, 65 in 2025, 35 between January and July 1, 2026.
  • Largest disclosed: $827 million into DAZN from Len Blavatnik's Access Industries; $10 billion into the Los Angeles Lakers from TWG Global, the family office of Mark Walters.
  • Single family office economics: launched at roughly $100 million net worth, $500,000 to $5 million a year to operate; Kerry Finn puts the range at $100 million to $250 million investable and $250 million to $500 million net worth.
  • Multi-family office: roughly $25 million to $250 million investable. Virtual family office: roughly $5 million to $40 million investable.
  • Lou Taylor, Tri Star Sports and Entertainment Group: "If you're an actor in Hollywood making $3 million a year, it's not cost effective for you to set up your own family office."
  • Entertainment services cited: structuring income streams, residuals and royalties, back-end participation planning, loan-out corporation management, production company acquisition or exit planning, slate financing and co-investments.
  • Carolyn Hunt, Barnes & Thornburg: family offices "are not managing outside limited-partner capital and generally face far less quarterly reporting pressure than private equity firms, hedge funds or banks."
  • Finn on allocation: on $100 million liquid, 20 to 30 percent may go to alternatives, so up to $30 million across IP, film deals and similar.
  • FINTRX database: roughly 4,500 family offices, more than 30,000 contacts, $50 million minimum asset threshold.

IndieWire compared two organized consumer campaigns from the same year. Coyote vs. Acme, the roughly $70 million film Warner Bros. Discovery shelved in November 2023 for an estimated $30 million tax write-down, was acquired by Ketchup Entertainment for a reported $50 million, opened August 28 to $15.9 million, dropped 28.8 percent to $11.3 million, and has reached $37 million domestic with an A CinemaScore. Paramount's Scream 7, boycotted after Spyglass Media Group fired Melissa Barrera, opened to a franchise-record $63.6 million in February and finished around $208 million worldwide on a 30 percent Rotten Tomatoes score.
Potential Talent Implication: A film its own studio valued at a write-down was worth $50 million to a buyer and has drawn $37 million from the audience that studio passed on, which is the number a filmmaker points to when negotiating a reversion right on a shelved title.
The Facts
  • Coyote vs. Acme: roughly $70 million budget, directed by Dave Green, script by Samy Burch, shelved by Warner Bros. Discovery in November 2023 for an estimated $30 million tax write-down.
  • Ketchup Entertainment acquired worldwide rights for a reported $50 million; released August 28, 2026.
  • Opening $15.9 million domestic; second weekend $11.3 million, down 28.8 percent; $14.5 million over the four-day Labor Day frame; $37 million domestic total.
  • Ketchup previously released the Looney Tunes title The Day the Earth Blew Up (2025).
  • Scream 7: Melissa Barrera fired by Spyglass in November 2023; Jenna Ortega and director Christopher Landon exited; film rebuilt around Neve Campbell.
  • Scream 7 opened to a franchise-record $63.6 million in February 2026, fell 73.3 percent in weekend two, finished around $208 million worldwide; 30 percent Rotten Tomatoes, 35 Metascore, 2.2-star Letterboxd average from more than 500,000 users.
  • Comparison points cited: Black Panther and Crazy Rich Asians grassroots ticket campaigns; Obsession, made for under $1 million, grossed more than $500 million worldwide.
  • If Paramount's stalled Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition closes, both studios sit inside one company.

Toronto Now Has a Formal Film Market, and AFM Has a Problem
TIFF will host roughly 200 private market screenings of titles not playing the festival, up from 50 to 100 in past years, with more than 6,000 market delegates attending.
TIFF has formalized its market for the first time. Festival director Cameron Bailey told IndieWire's Screen Talk podcast that Toronto will host roughly 200 private screenings of titles not in the festival, against 50 to 100 in past years, with more than 6,000 delegates and hundreds of sellers who have not attended TIFF in a decade. Sales agents told IndieWire the September date sits close to summer for packaging, and that European and Asian buyers cannot fly in twice in two months for both Toronto and AFM.

  • More than 6,000 market delegates, about 1,000 more than last year.
  • TIFF unveiled 50 titles as part of an international financing forum.
  • TIFF is providing screening rooms and office space and paying for many sellers to attend; hundreds of sellers are returning after a decade away.
  • Fewer Press and Industry screenings this year, often one per film instead of two, to make room for market screenings.

  • Last year's TIFF produced the most lucrative festival acquisition on record, Obsession.
  • AFM returned to Los Angeles after a year in Las Vegas; other domestic agents say AFM "isn't going anywhere."

British Producers Now Take More Money From Abroad Than From UK Broadcasters
UK broadcaster revenue fell 4.7 percent to £1.99 billion while international revenue rose 15.8 percent to £1.57 billion, and subscription streamers now place 72.3 percent of primary commissions from outside the UK.
The Pact Census for 2025 puts total UK independent producer revenue at £3.81 billion, up 4.1 percent, its second-highest total. UK television revenue fell 4.7 percent to £1.99 billion, below £2 billion for the first time since 2020 and a third consecutive year of decline. International revenue rose 15.8 percent to £1.57 billion, 41.1 percent of the total. The secondary rights market grew £65 million to £575 million. Pact chief executive Warner said broadcasters now contribute considerably less of the initial production cost, making retained rights more important to producers financing their own shows.
Potential Talent Implication: UK producers now fund more of the budget themselves and recoup through the secondary rights market, and the Terms of Trade that let them keep those rights on a British commission are what Channel 4, Sky, ITV and the BBC are all reopening.
The Facts
  • Total UK independent producer revenue 2025: £3.81 billion, up 4.1 percent, second-highest on record behind 2022's just under £4 billion.
  • UK television revenue: £1.99 billion, down 4.7 percent from £2.09 billion, below £2 billion for the first time since 2020.
  • International revenue: £1.57 billion, up 15.8 percent from £1.35 billion, 41.1 percent of total revenue, second only to 2022's £1.62 billion.
  • Subscription streamers now account for 72.3 percent of all primary commissions from outside the UK, £916 million, up from 27 percent a decade ago.
  • Secondary rights market: up £65 million to £575 million.
  • Non-TV revenue (online publishing, talent management, promotions, PR, feature films): £258 million, above the previous record of £236 million set in 2013.
  • Domestic network commissions have fallen for a third consecutive year, pressuring small and mid-sized production companies.
  • Causes cited: advertising market contraction, viewer shift away from broadcast, inflationary production costs.
  • The Terms of Trade, in place since 2003, let independent producers retain rights to shows commissioned by British networks. Channel 4 is working on an in-house division, Sky is buying ITV, and BBC Director General Matt Brittin has questioned whether the rules remain fit for purpose.
  • Pact closed a new Terms of Trade deal with Paramount's Channel 5 in March.
  • Pact CEO Warner on secondary rights growth: "It could also suggest that producers might be increasingly relying on future rights revenue to help finance production."
  • Warner on financing: "In an environment where indies are contributing ever more towards the cost of production in the first place, they need to be in the position to recoup that investment themselves, and the rights become even more important."
  • The BBC is seeking up to £500 million in cost savings. Pact again proposed replacing the licence fee with a household levy on the German model.
  • Warner replaced long-serving CEO John McVay in March 2026.

Netflix Spent Four Months Clearing Rights Before It Could Greenlight Lonesome Dove
Teton Ridge locked the four-book McMurtry rights in February 2025, took the Kazan and Stuart script out in late April, and closed with Netflix by early May, but gaps in the rights web delayed the greenlight until today.
Netflix has ordered Lonesome Dove straight to series from Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart with Teton Ridge Entertainment. Teton Ridge acquired the full Larry McMurtry tetralogy, which Puck reports took several years of untangling a chain of title running from Suzanne De Passe through a long list of later owners. The package went out in late April with two days of buyer meetings and landed at Netflix by early May. Deadline reports the four-month gap to greenlight came from gaps in the rights that had to be secured. Paramount never took a meeting.

The Facts
  • Netflix has greenlit Lonesome Dove straight to series, envisioned as an ongoing series, from co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart.

  • Teton Ridge developed in-house, then went out with the pilot script in late April 2026. Buyers were told Kazan and Stuart would meet interested parties over two days.
  • The package landed at Netflix by early May in a competitive situation. Confirmation took four months because of gaps in the necessary rights that had to be secured.

  • One rep quoted by Puck on Tull: "There were other people who wanted it, but Thomas was one of one in terms of how relentless he was in working things out."

  • Executive producers: Kazan, Stuart, Thomas Tull, Jillian Share and Jen Gorton of Teton Ridge, Jon Jashni, Diana Ossana, and Curtis McMurtry of the McMurtry Estate.

  • The 1989 four-part miniseries starred Robert Duvall, Tommy Lee Jones, Danny Glover, Diane Lane and Anjelica Huston, and ran on CBS.
  • Puck notes Paramount+ allowed Taylor Sheridan to move to Universal.

Christine Is Stuck Inside Three Bankruptcies and Nobody Can Say Who Owns It
Rebecca Hall's 2016 drama is not being licensed to streamers or cable until a chain of title is re-established, and its filmmakers say they cannot get an answer from trustees in two countries.
Christine, the 2016 drama starring Rebecca Hall as news anchor Christine Chubbuck, is caught in overlapping bankruptcies and cannot be licensed. Distributor The Orchard became 1091 Media in 2019 when Sony divested, was bought by Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment in 2022, and went into Chapter 7 liquidation two years later. The filmmakers then learned the film's London financier Great Point Media had also gone bankrupt after founder Jim Reeve's death. Writer-producer Craig Shilowich says some or all of the rights sit inside the case and that trustees in two countries will not respond.
Potential Talent Implication: Christine built an audience on Netflix and is now unlicensable because no one can establish who holds the rights, which is what a reversion trigger tied to a distributor's insolvency exists to prevent.
The Facts
  • Christine premiered at Sundance in 2016. The Orchard bought U.S. distribution rights. It was nominated for Independent Spirit honors and won critics group prizes.
  • Hall: "It feels terrible because this is definitely a film and a performance that I'm incredibly proud of, and I know that it means a lot to a lot of people. So the idea that it could just sort of disappear is insane to me."
  • Hall on the release: "They didn't have the resources to capitalize on the acclaim and the other accolades that the film received. They just couldn't afford to market it in a big way, so the release suffered from that."
  • The Orchard ran a filmmaker portal showing box office plus digital sales and rentals. Shilowich: "They were like 'this is our thing, we're going to demystify film accounting.' They had a portal for filmmakers where you could see all the receipts coming in and out, and that was rare."
  • 2019: The Orchard rebranded as 1091 Media; principal backer Sony divested. The portal began going down frequently. Shilowich: "It became a promise that they didn't keep over time."
  • 2022: Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment bought 1091 Media and its library.
  • 2024: Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment failed and entered Chapter 7 liquidation.
  • The filmmakers then discovered Great Point Media, the London-based financier of Christine, had gone bankrupt following founder Jim Reeve's death.
  • Shilowich: "There was essentially no one to talk to about the fate of our film except for government-appointed bankruptcy trustees in two different countries. And there are a bunch of other smaller distribution outlets, like Redbox, the DVD kiosk company, involved. So it's actually a very large, extremely complex bankruptcy case, and some or all of our rights are involved."
  • Shilowich on trying to buy it back: "If the creditors aren't claiming it, I want to know, 'Well, can I have it? Can I buy it?' We're not only unable to get a satisfactory answer, but really to receive any response."
  • Until a chain of title is re-established, Christine, which previously built an audience on Netflix, is not being licensed to streamers or cable.
  • Director Antonio Campos: "I had this naive belief that when you sold your film to some place, they would take care of it. The person that's going to care the most about your work is you."
  • The filmmakers have spoken with other filmmakers whose work is caught in the same bankruptcies.
  • A tenth anniversary screening was held at Telluride, with additional screenings at Brooklyn's Nitehawk Cinema and the Jacob Burns Film Center.

The BBC Says a 1 Percent Raise Costs 180 Jobs
Bectu and the National Union of Journalists rejected an offer the BBC puts at an average 2.1 percent and the unions put at 1.5 percent basic, against UK inflation of 2.8 percent.
BBC director general Matt Brittin told an internal town hall that unions rejected the corporation's improved pay offer, raising the prospect of a mass staff walkout. The BBC revised its offer from 1 percent to an average of 2.1 percent, though unions said the basic offer was 1.5 percent against UK inflation of 2.8 percent. Brittin said a 1 percent rise equals 180 jobs and that the BBC is cutting £500 million ($675 million) on top of an earlier £1.5 billion target. Bectu head Philippa Childs said staff morale is at rock bottom.

The Facts
  • Offer revised from 1 percent to an average of 2.1 percent; unions say the basic offer is 1.5 percent. Some employees would get 2.5 percent, weighted to low earners. Top leadership gets no rise.
  • UK inflation cited at 2.8 percent.
  • Unions rejecting: Bectu and the National Union of Journalists. Any industrial action would require a ballot of members.
  • Brittin: "That was disappointing. I understand the cost of living and the pressures that people are under."
  • Brittin on the trade-off: a 1 percent pay rise is equivalent to 180 jobs. "The cupboard is bare. There isn't a cash reserve that we can draw on here."
  • Savings target: £500 million ($675 million), expanding on a previous £1.5 billion goal. More detail on cuts due in coming weeks.
  • Charter renewal talks with the government are unresolved, so future funding is uncertain.
  • Philippa Childs, Bectu: "In the middle of a cost-of-living-crisis a pay rise significantly below inflation, coupled with a detriment to other terms and conditions, is clearly unacceptable to our members."
  • Brittin, a former Google executive, earns £565,000.
  • 94 percent of the UK population uses the BBC monthly; fewer than 80 percent pay the £180 annual licence fee.

Streaming Is Raising Prices Faster Than Cable Ever Did
Apple TV's price has tripled since 2019, Disney+ is up 172 percent, and eight ad free major streamers now cost about $151 a month against $90 four years ago.
The Hollywood Reporter compared streamer pricing against Bureau of Labor Statistics data and found streaming rates rose 11.8 percent over the past twelve months, against an annual average of 3.9 percent for cable and satellite. Since 2022, streaming prices have risen more than three times as fast as inflation. Apple TV launched at $4.99 in 2019 and now costs $15, half of that increase coming in the past year. Peacock's tiers rose about 50 percent. HBO Max is the outlier, up 23 percent over six years.
Potential Talent Implication: The money is coming from pricing, not growth, so the question for talent with backend on a streaming title becomes how streaming revenue is defined and shared.
The Facts
  • Streaming rates collectively rose 11.8 percent over the past 12 months. The biggest single year was 2023, at an average 17.7 percent.
  • THR's analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data puts cable and satellite price growth at an annual average of 3.9 percent, excluding the late 1980s deregulation surge that peaked at 14 percent.
  • Apple TV: launched at $4.99 in 2019, now $15. Up 200 percent, with a 50 percent rise in the past year alone.
  • Disney+: launched at $6.99 with no ads in 2019, now $11.99 with ads. Up 172 percent on launch price.
  • Paramount+: cheapest tier up 80 percent in five years.
  • Netflix Premium: up 125 percent since 2013.
  • Peacock: tiers up roughly 50 percent recently. HBO Premium is $3 more than Peacock Premium Plus.
  • HBO Max: up 23 percent over six years, the smallest increase in the set.
  • Eight major streamers without ads or bundle commitments: about $151 a month, versus roughly $90 four years ago.
  • Consumer prices have risen an average of 3.84 percent annually since 2019, a 33 percent cumulative increase in cost of living.
  • Fully loaded cable bundles from Spectrum and DirecTV run north of $170 a month.

The Summer Box Office Hit $4.76 Billion and Admissions Rose With It
US summer box office reached an all-time record $4.76 billion, with admissions above 322 million against 275 million last summer, the first summer where all four core months each cleared $1 billion.
Rentrak has the May 1 to September 7 domestic frame at $4.76 billion, the highest on record, with each core month topping $1 billion for the first time. Price alone does not explain it: EntTelligence counts admissions above 322 million against 275 million in summer 2025, on an average adult ticket of $13.46. Universal led distributors at $1.23 billion, up 63 percent, ahead of Disney at $1.034 billion and Sony at $1 billion. Greenlight Analytics says the top 15 fall titles track 3.5 points ahead of last year.
Potential Talent Implication: Theatrical grosses grew on attendance rather than ticket-price inflation, so box office bonuses, cash breakeven and first-dollar-gross definitions are being negotiated against a market that is genuinely larger, and the two biggest breakouts were directed by filmmakers who came from YouTube.
The Facts
  • Record domestic summer of $4.76 billion for May 1 to September 7, per Rentrak. Variety separately reported the figure as $4.67 billion.
  • First summer on record where each of the four core months cleared $1 billion: May $1.07B, June $1.08B, July $1.18B, August $1.276B.
  • Admissions above 322 million versus summer 2025's 275 million, per EntTelligence. Average ticket prices: adult $13.46, child $11.51, adult premium large format $18.39.
  • Distributor share for the period: Universal $1.23B (+63%), Disney $1.034B (-2%), Sony $1B (+459%), Lionsgate $270M (+296%), Warner Bros $239.3M (-76%), Paramount $219.8M (-21%), Amazon MGM $170.1M (+400%).

France and Korea Pledged $1.16 Billion for the Screen Industries Through 2031
The same summit launched IRIS, a fund for independent cinemas and distributors, with Jane Campion, Pedro Almodovar, Jim Jarmusch and Tilda Swinton on its council.
Emmanuel Macron and Korean President Lee Jae Myung announced the 1 billion euro commitment on Monday at the Lumiere Summit in Saint Paul de Vence, covering 2027 through 2031. The two said other countries may join if they accept the partnership's commitments on human creativity, copyright protection and cultural diversity. France separately launched the International Resilience Initiative for Independent Screens, or IRIS, which targets independent distributors, cinemas and nonprofit networks rather than production. Ted Sarandos, Donna Langley, Bryan Lourd and George Clooney were among more than 200 attendees.
Potential Talent Implication: State money aimed at distribution and exhibition rather than production could give filmmakers a theatrical route that does not require selling worldwide rights to a studio or streamer, which is worth pricing into a territory by territory rights strategy.
The Facts
  • France and Korea pledged 1 billion euros, about $1.16 billion, to the global screen industries from 2027 to 2031.
  • Announced Monday, September 7, at the Lumiere Summit at the Fondation Maeght in Saint Paul de Vence, co-hosted by Macron and Lee Jae Myung, who is on a four day state visit to France.
  • Lee said Korea would take the lead "in producing content which resonates with humanity and transcends borders and language barriers."
  • Other countries are welcome to join on the condition they sign up to commitments on human creativity, copyright protection and cultural diversity.
  • IRIS is described in summit materials as "the first international mechanism dedicated to the circulation of independent cinema, combining funding, expertise and advocacy," with the ability to "intervene rapidly when an independent cinema, distributor or nonprofit network is at risk."
  • Summit materials state the gap directly: independent distribution and exhibition "receive far less support, nationally and internationally, than production."
  • IRIS international council signatories include Richard Linklater, Rebecca Zlotkowski, Jafar Panahi, Jane Campion, Pedro Almodovar, Wim Wenders, Tarik Saleh, Jia Zhang-ke, Agnieszka Holland, Costa-Gavras, Jim Jarmusch, Tilda Swinton, Juliette Binoche, Vicky Krieps, Ira Sachs, Ruben Ostlund, Kaouther Ben Hania and Thomas Vinterberg.
  • France is also establishing a "Lumiere Alliance" of national film agencies and public bodies, meeting twice a year, once around Cannes in May and once in a rotating host country.
  • Macron will host a follow up gathering on IRIS in New York on September 22.
  • Attendees included Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, NBCUniversal chair Donna Langley, CAA head Bryan Lourd, George Clooney, Mediawan co-founder Pierre-Antoine Capton, Canal+ Group CEO Maxime Saada and Cannes director Thierry Fremaux.

Macron Wants YouTube Paying Into the Content Funds Netflix Already Pays
Macron told Variety that YouTube should be brought into the same local-investment obligations as Netflix, Amazon and Disney, and that France will require AI-generated content to be labelled.
French President Emmanuel Macron, speaking to Variety at the Lumière Summit he co-chaired with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, said YouTube "is de facto the default platform in a lot of countries" and diverts audiences from channels where "a lot of money is invested in creation." He argued YouTube should be brought into the same ecosystem as Netflix, Amazon and Disney, already required to invest in local production. On AI he said labelling is non-negotiable: "When you have content produced by AI, you just have to know it."
Potential Talent Implication: Local-content investment obligations are what turn a platform into a commissioning buyer, so extending them to YouTube would create a funded market for work that today earns only ad revenue share, and mandatory AI labelling gives authors a disclosure right to negotiate against.
The Facts
  • Macron co-chaired the Lumière Summit at the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Monday.
  • Macron on YouTube: "YouTube is very efficient. It's de facto the default platform in a lot of countries for a lot of people. And it's quite clear that today they divert a lot of people from these platforms or the big channels where a lot of money is invested in creation."
  • Variety reports YouTube is currently outperforming Netflix in over 20 international markets.
  • Macron said countries need to "engage with them" multilaterally so the platform helps finance "local content," while supporting "more creativity, more creations, more respect of the authors."
  • On AI: "When you have content produced by AI, you just have to know it. So transparency for us is key. We want to flag when the content is produced with AI. Because we think it's fair." He warned that without it AI could "totally transform the relationship to truth."
  • On the Paramount-Warner Bros. deal, Macron said he had no active lobbying role but supported "the commitments made to invest more in Europe and to create more content and to provide guarantees and commitments vis-à-vis our theaters." He called the case fundamentally "a U.S. M&A story."
  • Paramount Skydance boss David Ellison met Macron in Paris in January. Ellison was not at the Summit; Paramount Skydance's Andy Gordon sat at Macron's lunch table alongside Disney's Dana Walden, Netflix's Ted Sarandos, NBCUniversal Entertainment's Donna Langley, Mediawan's Pierre-Antoine Capton and Sony's Tom Rothman.
  • Macron named France's international tax credit as the policy he most wants to survive his term. It was recently strengthened to include above-the-line costs.
  • "We improved tax credits, international tax credits. If somebody wants to withdraw this tax credit, it will just kill the industry and a lot of opportunities."
  • Emily in Paris season six and The White Lotus season four are currently shooting in France.
  • Macron leaves office in May. He warned that "some extremes are fighting very hard against the CNC and what we call this exception culturelle." France's system levies cinema admissions, collected by the CNC and re-injected into local production.

Venice's Director Says Studios Are Using AI and Not Saying So
Barbera said AI is cheaper and faster than CGI and can be better, and that this year's Venice official selection includes a documentary made almost entirely with AI.
Alberto Barbera, artistic director of the Venice Film Festival, told Deadline at the festival's midpoint that many filmmakers and studios are using AI without disclosing it. He compared the shift to the digital revolution of the late 1990s and said its impact will be far greater, adding that the debate so far has covered only the negative consequences. Venice's opening film, Danny Boyle's Ink, used AI, and an almost entirely AI made documentary sits in official selection. Barbera has two years left on his contract after this edition.
Potential Talent Implication: If undisclosed AI use is already common on studio productions, disclosure and consent language in performer, writer and director agreements may be worth more than compensation terms negotiated afterward, because a use nobody knows happened cannot be priced.
The Facts
  • Barbera, on AI: "We know that many filmmakers and studios are using A.I. without disclosing it. It's cheaper, faster and it can be better than CGI."
  • He compared the moment to the digital revolution at the end of the 1990s: "people were reluctant to admit that it would be a revolution for the business but within a few years it had completely changed. We're going through that now. And yet, the impact of A.I. will be far greater."
  • Danny Boyle has said he used AI in making Venice opener Ink. A documentary "almost entirely made with A.I." is in official selection for the first time.
  • On studios skipping Venice: "They will come back. There's no question about that. The only reason they're not here is that the films weren't ready." He named Digger as the only ready film that chose not to do festivals, and said Fincher's film and The Social Reckoning were still shooting or reshooting in August.
  • On festival cost as a deterrent: "You have a film that costs $300M, you spend another $100M on marketing. An extra $1M to go to Venice is nothing."
  • On films that opened well without a festival launch, including Sinners, Backrooms, The Odyssey and Marty Supreme: "Most of these weren't ready for a big festival and they were mostly big and happy surprises at the box office."
  • On audiences: "the audiences in cinemas are getting younger and younger. This will change how films are released and what films are made."
  • Two films in this year's Competition were directed by women, one of them a co-director. Barbera said 50 percent of the selection committee are women and rejected a dedicated section as "a ghetto for women."
  • Barbera is 76 and has two years remaining on his contract after this edition.

California Pays No Incentive on Star Salaries, and That Is What Keeps Features Out
Whalefall took nearly $11 million in California credits on $50 million of qualified spend, and its producer says the state's exclusion of above-the-line costs is why star-driven features still shoot elsewhere.
20th Century Studios shot Whalefall in California, from Monterey to San Pedro and then Radford Studios, for 62 days with 11 cast and 180 crew. The production received nearly $11 million in tax credits on $50 million in qualified expenditures. Executive producer Doug Merrifield priced Louisiana against California beforehand and found Louisiana only six figures cheaper, a gap he said would have vanished once specialists were flown in. California grants no incentive on above-the-line costs, and Merrifield offset that with post and visual effects spend. He said features will not return in volume without an above-the-line credit.
Potential Talent Implication: Above-the-line covers the cast and director fees, so a state incentive that excludes it prices a star salary as pure cost with no offset, and the location of the shoot turns on how large those fees are relative to post and visual effects spend.
The Facts
  • Whalefall stars Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily Rudd, directed by Brian Duffield from Daniel Kraus' novel, for 20th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment. In theaters October 16.
  • The production received nearly $11 million in tax credits on $50 million total qualified expenditures across a shoot scheduled for 50 days that became 62.
  • Executive producer Doug Merrifield: "On paper, Louisiana was a little cheaper, six figures cheaper, not seven figures cheaper, but at the end of the day, we were able to convince 20th Century that the best creative teams are here for this kind of picture."
  • Merrifield on the structure: "In California, you don't get an incentive on above the line, but we had enough in post and visual effects to offset the loss of what we didn't get from above the line."
  • Merrifield on what features still need: "if we want more feature work here, we're going to have to have some sort of ATL (above the line) incentive credit, which you don't get here right now. So if you have a big above the line, it doesn't make sense to shoot here."
  • On stage availability: "We were fortunate that it is at this time we were able to make such a good deal. But unfortunately, it is because it's so slow right now."
  • Imagine producer Allen Mendelbaum: "It's so unfortunately rare to have the opportunity to shoot here, that when people know that a movie's shooting in L.A., that is their first choice. They can come home at night, see their families and everything."
  • Whale stomach models were built by Wētā Workshop in New Zealand; the 12-foot-tall, 18-foot-long head, throat, esophagus and larynx were built in California by StudioArt & Technology because they were too large to ship in time.
  • California's Film & TV Tax Credit program rose to $750 million annually. Whalefall benefited from a $330 million funding round that preceded the expansion.
  • Over the summer, 41 films received $187 million in incentives, including Ben Affleck's Gingerbread Men, produced with Matt Damon under their Artists Equity banner, and Disney's Hexed.
  • Last July the California Film Commission allocated $40 million to Dan Fogelman ($20.8M) and Ryan Murphy ($17.9M) for television projects.
  • Other California shoots cited: Paul Thomas Anderson's $140 million One Battle After Another, Netflix's The Further Mis-adventures of Cliff Booth ($105.9M qualified spend), the 13 Going on 30 reboot at Netflix ($10.9M credit on $31.2M qualified) and They Follow ($7M on $20M).
  • A 35 percent postproduction incentive has been part of recent efforts to move work back to the state. President Donald Trump has voiced intentions to back a federal film and TV tax credit.
  • California's current application cycles close in September for features and independent productions, and run into October for television series.

George Clooney Says AI Will Take Below-the-Line Jobs First
Clooney told The Ankler at the Lumière Summit that his AI concern is below-the-line work, naming film scoring as a craft that generative tools can already substitute at the low-budget end.
George Clooney, at the Lumière Summit hosted by Emmanuel Macron and Lee Jae Myung, told The Ankler his central worry about AI is below-the-line employment, not star-level work. He used composing as the example: someone requests a score in the style of Alexandre Desplat that is "good enough for some low-budget television show" without being Desplat or triggering a suit. Clooney said the industry missed its moment: "We're all way behind the eight ball. We should have been ahead of this, but it happened really quickly." He framed the question as containment, not prevention: "the train has left the station."
Potential Talent Implication: Style imitation that stops short of copying a specific work sits outside what copyright reliably reaches, so the protection for a composer or below-the-line artist runs through contract terms covering training use and style replication rather than through infringement claims after the fact.
The Facts
  • Clooney spoke to The Ankler's Claire Atkinson at Monday's Lumière Festival in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
  • The summit gathered artists, producers, Hollywood executives and political leaders, alongside a $1 billion initiative to support independent film. AI was the central theme.
  • Clooney: "I had a really interesting dinner with President Macron, talking about the emergence of AI as it's becoming a revolution in our industry. I'm more worried about below-the-line jobs, quite honestly, which is going to be a real concern."
  • On scoring, referencing French composer Alexandre Desplat: "somebody goes online and says, 'Give me an Alexander Desplat score that won't get me sued,' and it's not Alexander Desplat, but it's good enough for some low-budget television show for sure."
  • "So there's an awful lot of things that are going to make it very difficult for the people who've been doing this for a long time to make a living."
  • On guardrails: "It's also very difficult to stop it, right? It's going. The train has left the station, and so the questions are going to be: How do you incorporate it? And are there versions where you can say, this you can't do? We're all way behind the eight ball."
  • Clooney also spoke about AI at the Venice Film Festival the previous week.

The Federal Film Credit Would Pay Off Most in Georgia and Louisiana
Georgia's film and TV spending fell from $4.4 billion in 2022 to $2 billion last fiscal year, and Louisiana has lost 52.7 percent of its film jobs since 2021.
Sam Roseme, an entertainment partner at Reed Smith, argues in The Hollywood Reporter that the federal production credit Trump has called for is not a Los Angeles subsidy but a rescue for the states that absorbed the production exodus. Georgia fell from a $4.4 billion peak in film and TV spending in 2022 to $2 billion last fiscal year, with productions down from 412 to 280. Louisiana production dropped roughly 65 percent in three years. Reported drafts point to a base credit near 20 percent on qualified domestic spending, stackable on state incentives.
Potential Talent Implication: A federal credit stacked on state incentives could reset where a picture can afford to shoot, giving talent room to negotiate domestic locations, shorter travel and residency terms instead of accepting a London or Vancouver schedule.
The Facts
  • Trump called on Congress in a Truth Social post to draft and pass "The Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act."
  • Georgia: peak of $4.4 billion in film and TV production spending in 2022, down to $2 billion in the last fiscal year, a 10-year low. Total productions fell from 412 to 280. State incentive up to 30 percent.
  • Louisiana: production down roughly 65 percent over a three-year period; 52.7 percent of film jobs lost since 2021, the largest percentage decline in the country. State incentive up to 40 percent.
  • United Kingdom: 40 percent tax credit backed by the national treasury, plus large soundstage capacity.
  • Canada: a 25 percent federal credit stacks on provincial credits of 25 to 45 percent, exceeding 50 percent combined in British Columbia and Ontario.
  • Roughly 80 countries offer a national tax credit. The United States does not.
  • Reported drafts: a base credit of around 20 percent on qualified domestic spending, potentially with bonuses for productions filming in underserved regions or completing post-production domestically, stackable on state incentives.
  • Worked example in the piece: Georgia's 30 percent plus a 20 percent federal credit reaches 50 percent, matching Canada.
  • Florida let its production incentive lapse in 2016 and saw production fall significantly.
  • The author is Sam Roseme, a partner in Reed Smith's Century City office.

  • Asia: nearly 35 percent of Netflix's international titles in the US come from Japan or South Korea, more than twice Prime Video's share from those markets.

Vertical Dramas Pay Like Guest Roles and Carry No Residuals
TJ Wilk earned just over $3,000 on his first microdrama and $17,500 for seven days in China this year. His agent says top vertical rates match a top-of-show guest credit, with no residuals.
TJ Wilk has filmed more than 30 mobile-first microdramas since 2023 and now works as an actor full time. He made just over $3,000 for 10 to 11 days on his first vertical and $17,500 for a seven-day shoot in China this year, and earned $90,000 from verticals in 2025. His agent, Tina Contogenis of Eris Talent Agency, which represents about 100 vertical actors, says top rates match what a guest actor with top-of-show credit makes on a TV series but carry no residuals. Most vertical productions are non-union.
Potential Talent Implication: A lane that pays like a guest role and returns nothing after delivery makes the upfront number the entire deal, so reuse limits, any residual participation and consent over AI-generated performance are the terms worth pressing while the format's rates are still being set.
The Facts
  • Microdramas are shot vertically for phones, cram a feature's worth of story into a seven- to 10-day shoot, and typically cost around $300,000. Wilk: "there will be 120 pages or more of script, and I've got like four days to memorize it."
  • Wilk's pay: just over $3,000 for 10 to 11 days on his first microdrama; $17,500 for seven days on a recent China project; $90,000 in total vertical earnings in 2025.
  • Tina Contogenis, founder of Eris Talent Agency, which represents around 100 actors in the vertical space, says these rates for top vertical actors are in line with what a guest actor with top-of-show credit might make on a TV series. "There are no residuals," she notes.
  • Verticals are typically non-union. SAG-AFTRA created a microdrama agreement last fall covering productions with budgets under $300,000, establishing a minimum salary for lead performers of $250 for an eight-hour day. It is not clear how widely it is being used. Digital video professionals have said union standards would make the economics unworkable.
  • ReelShort tops the international verticals market with a 29 percent share per Media Partners Asia, is projected to do $1 billion in revenue this year with an estimated $40 million net profit, and verticals overall are on track to be a $3.6 billion industry outside China.
  • Wilk's first vertical, the 56-episode Her Desired Alphas, has 28.8 million views on ReelShort. Drowning in His Restraint, released on TikTok and LoveShots in March, has more than 1.6 billion views.
  • More than 120,000 microdramas were released in China in the first three months of 2026, and 95 percent featured computer-generated talent, per CNN citing Chinese state media.
